Criticals

One row per location of the table in force, with six pips. Click a pip to set that severity, and click the standing pip to step back one. The row prints what the standing severity does.

The control under the rows is the procedure: pick the location, which is your own 2D roll, type the attack's Effect and press Apply. Severity comes from the Effect (Core p.140). An Effect under 6 is refused. The sheet handles repeats according to the rules in force, and an Effect-driven critical that raises Hull Severity does so here too.

Hull Severity is a separate track, since many cells raise it rather than damaging the location hit. Under the Core rules it reads out beside the DMs, and you can type it in Edit.

The Control DM and Systems DM readouts total what the standing criticals impose. The Control DM feeds the two combat actions by itself. Criticals that cost Speed Bands reach the band in play. Most other effects are sentences for you to apply.

Under the Handbook's rules the line also carries Structure, a tenth of the Hull rounded up unless Structure in the header's Edit form states one, how many times Structure has been exceeded, with the disabled state at ten and worse beyond (VH2026 p.6-7), and the cost of repairs. It also shows the DM a sensor check gets against this vehicle, and what size of weapon an Effect critical now needs. Collision opens the collision procedure, which asks what was hit and at what speed, then applies the criticals it raises and reports the occupants' damage (VH2026 p.11-12).

A Hull critical of Severity 5 or 6 halves the Structure, rounded up, each time one is applied (VH2026 p.9-10). That is the critical control's and a collision's work; a pip clicked by hand halves nothing.

The eraser in the heading, in Edit, clears the standing criticals of both books. It leaves the Structure, which comes back by a repair of its own (VH2026 p.11): lower Structure halved in the same block once that repair is made. Comfort, in the header's Edit form, is the level the statline prints with its effect (VH2026 p.24).

Traits and the rest

Trait chips work as elsewhere, in the vehicle vocabulary. Open Vehicle, AFV, ATV, Off-Roader, Tracked, Responsive, Unresponsive and VTOL all change something on this sheet.

Sub-type detail in Edit switches on two optional blocks: Submersible, for safe and crush depth and life support, and Remote, for a drone's interface and its two ranges. A drone can be within control range and out of telemetry range. Each block is absent rather than zero until ticked, and unticking discards what it held.

The Cross-check panel appears once Spaces is filled in. It compares Shipping, Cargo and Hull per Space against what the design rules would give. A disagreeing row flags and never rewrites: the printed number wins, and plenty of published vehicles disagree. For an airship it also reports the gas envelope.

The header and the rail

The header is read-only in both modes. It shows what the ship can do this minute, not what it was built to do:

  • Hull is the pool, value over maximum. Clicking it, or the broken heart at the end of the line, opens the damage dialog, which takes off or gives back points with no armour involved. Repairs are made here.
  • Armour is the armour left after criticals, plus the hull's own Protection.
  • Thrust is the current figure, criticals folded in. Jump is the rating.
  • Power is what is left over, in the same units as the plant.
  • Fuel is the level in the tank over the tank's size, and how many jumps at the rated range that buys. A new hull's tank is empty until you fill it on the voyage screen.
  • Crew is the bodies aboard over the crew the ship requires, with the Pilot level of whoever is linked at the pilot station. A station counts for its number, so Engineers ×2 is two, and the figure turns red while the ship is short.
  • Initiative is that Pilot level plus current Thrust plus any standing DM. Holographic controls add theirs here (Core p.186).
  • Control DM, Sensor DM and Jump DM appear only while a critical is imposing one.

Three flags can sit under the name. Wrecked is set by itself when the hull reaches zero; the book gives a ship no state below that (Core p.168). Scans unarmed appears when every mount is a pop-up (High Guard p.28). Maintenance overdue counts periods since the last service stamp, read against the campaign day. It changes no number anywhere.

The rail beside the tabs carries the Hull track and four budgets, and it stays in view whichever tab is open.

Tonnage adds up every fitting against the hull. Hardpoints counts mounts against one per full 100 tons (High Guard p.26), and under it sit firmpoints and airlocks. These are red lines and never refusals: published ships break them, and the sheet lets you save whatever the page prints.

Power is the one budget with a state. Each consumer has a switch, and taking one offline frees its draw, which is the Engineer's action of Core p.171. A red Brownout means the draw exceeds what the plant is putting out. A Power Plant critical lowers the output, and the rail says by how much.

Manoeuvre lists the seven range bands with what a change out of each costs at the ship's current Thrust (Core p.166), how many rounds it takes when one round cannot pay, and the attack DM, or dogfight where the book prints none. An M-Drive critical shows up here as bands going out of reach.

A hull with a second drive gets a chip here that lights it. Lit, its Thrust adds to the total and the rail states the G the compensators do not cover, with the check it costs the crew (High Guard p.16, p.45, p.47). You decide when it burns and when it stops; nothing schedules it.

Design: hull and drives

The Design tab holds what the sheet is built from. In edit mode you type hull tons, configuration, armour material and points, Thrust, Jump, power plant output, bridge type, holographic controls, sensors, Tech Level, the size of the fuel tank, the cargo hold, a second drive's Thrust, and two ticks: Reaction drive says the ship's own Thrust is a reaction drive, and refined says what kind of fuel is in the tank. Unrefined fuel costs DM−2 on the jump.

From those the sheet derives Hull points (High Guard p.10-12), armour tonnage, cost and cap (High Guard p.12-13), drive tonnages (High Guard p.16), bridge tonnage and cost (High Guard p.19), and every row of the power panel (High Guard p.17).

Do not type a printed Hull figure into the Hull characteristic. On a ship it stays at 0, because the points derive, and anything written there is added to them. A vehicle works the other way round. The Printed figures block is the place.

Printed figures

A formula is a default; a published statblock is data. Six figures can be overridden: Hull points, armour tonnage, bridge tonnage, bridge cost, fuel per jump and power draw. Leave a box empty and the formula answers, with its result greyed in the box. Type the page's figure and that wins, marked printed wherever it appears.

Two of them mean less than they seem to. A printed power draw is the full-power total, and switching a consumer off goes on subtracting from it. A printed fuel-per-jump is design tonnage, and what a jump actually burns stays at Core p.157's rate.

Hull options

Two rows of chips. The first are the hull's own options, which stack (High Guard p.12); the second are options installed on it, each priced per ton of hull (High Guard p.13-14). Click to switch one on or off, and pick a Stealth type if Stealth is fitted. A size limit, a Tech Level or a clashing pair is drawn as a red line under the block and refuses nothing. Reflec adds its Protection only against a weapon whose damage type says laser.

Mounts and weapons

A mount is not packaging. It holds the magazine and the position, and it multiplies damage by up to a thousand. Add one, choose its type, give it a position such as Dorsal turret, tick pop-up if it is concealed, then pick its weapons from the list. That list is the weapon Items on this ship, so add them first: drop one on the sheet, or use the crosshair control. A weapon's scale must be Spacecraft, and its traits must use the ship-weapon family, or they resolve to nothing with no message. @UUID[Compendium.mgt2.demo-items.Item.demoWeaponTurret]{Demo — Turret Laser} is filled in correctly.

Screens share the block. In edit mode the shield beside the + adds a row: choose the type and how many. A screen has no mount; it costs tonnage and Power, joins the gunners the hull needs, and is a pool in a fleet battle.

Crew

The roster holds stations, not people. A capital ship is crewed in the thousands, so a row can say Gunners ×40, and a row can be held by a name alone.

To build one, give the ship its role Items, the type the Items directory calls Crew Station, then add a station and choose its role. That list reads the ship and nothing else: a role made in the Items directory, or kept in a compendium, appears in it only once it is dropped on the ship. @UUID[Compendium.mgt2.demo-items.Item.demoRolePilot001]{Demo — Pilot} and @UUID[Compendium.mgt2.demo-items.Item.demoRoleGunner01]{Demo — Gunner} show what a role carries. The role's Crew position field is how the system finds the pilot, the astrogator and the engineer. Left empty, the role's name is tried against the same list, so a role called Helm with no Crew position is nobody's pilot.

In edit mode, the Station roles fold under the roster lists the ship's roles, each with its Crew position, its department and how many stations use it. Its New role button creates a blank role on the ship, so a role for one ship never needs the Items directory, and while the ship has none the fold says how to get one. The pencil opens the role, and an edit there changes this ship only. The trash removes it: every station that used it is left with no role but keeps its name, its crew member and its count, and a notice says how many stations that was. A station holds the role itself and not its name, so two roles called Pilot are two roles, which the fold and the station's list number Pilot (1) and Pilot (2).

A role dropped on the ship is a copy, and editing the original afterwards does not change it. Drop a role on a station row and that station takes it; if a copy of the same original is already aboard, the station takes that one and no second copy is made. Dropped anywhere else on the sheet, a role is simply added. To bring a later edit across, press Update from its source on the role's row in the fold: the copy takes the original's name, image and content, and its stations keep it. The control shows only while the original can still be found, so a copy whose original was deleted has none, and neither does one made by an earlier version of the system.

Drop a character or an NPC on a row and they take that station; drop one elsewhere on the table and they get a new row. Only those two Actor types are accepted. The mount field names where a gunner sits: a mount's position label, or its number counting from 1.

The buttons on a row are the role's actions, each one a check:

  • A skill action needs a linked sheet to read the level from, and is disabled on a vacant or name-only row.
  • A weapon action does too, and also needs the mount field filled and a weapon in that mount. It carries the damage payload to the chat card.
  • A special action on a vacant row only tells you it is the referee's call.

Each check opens @UUID[Compendium.mgt2.guide.JournalEntry.3wd9e5Iz4A9besSS.JournalEntryPage.AFpVHfj7ijV7S9ct]{the ordinary roll prompt}, seeded from the crew member. What the ship contributes rides it as modifiers you can untick: the role's own DM, the weapon's fire control, the Sensor DM on a sensors check, the Control DM on a Pilot check, a command bridge's DM on Tactics (naval).

Crew skill is typed, never averaged (High Guard p.110). It feeds the fleet rules, and it is stored whether or not they are on. Observed beside it is the average the roster can actually read, with a count of how many bodies it could not.

This block records what has happened to the ship. Nothing here rolls a location for you, and nothing fires a critical by itself.

The damage card writes the wound and stops there. Computer

Type the Processing score, and a backup's if there is one, with the two designations for each: /bis reserves +5 for Jump Control programs only, and /fib hardens the computer against ion weapons (High Guard p.20). The primary and the backup never run together. A chip selects which one is in service, and its Processing and designations are then the ones that count. A backup at or above the primary's score is a design failure and nothing more.

Ship software is a component Item of category Software, and its rating is the rating: Evade/2 is a component named Evade with rating 2. A package aboard spends no Processing until its box is ticked. A hull may carry more Bandwidth than it can run, which High Guard p.73 designs to, so the budget counts only what is started, and the hint under it states the difference. The box is a matter of budget only: the fleet figures read every package fitted, started or not.

A program above the hull's Tech Level does not run, because the operating Tech Level is the ship's and not the computer's. Overload says more is started than the computer can hold; the programs stay started, and the rest is yours to rule.

The parts list

The second block of the Design tab is a list of component Items, and no rating above reads it. The ratings are the ship; this is a transcription of its printed design, and you may leave it empty. Three things do look here: software, the automation part, and the fleet Traits, which go by the words in a component's name. @UUID[Compendium.mgt2.demo-items.Item.demoComponentFul]{Demo — Fuel Processor} shows a part filled in.

Where the Ship design checks rule is on, a ledger folds out under it. It reads power, tonnage, hardpoints and jump fuel off the parts, then holds the parts against the stored ratings, then checks the backup computer and any claim to be Hardened. A check with nothing to read is drawn and silent, so a parts list with no fuel row is not a ship short of fuel. Published ships fail these, and failing changes nothing.

Hold and passengers

Accommodation is the staterooms, the low berths and four passenger counts. The berths cost tonnage, and all of it feeds life support and the steward requirement. The passenger counts are a stand-in for a table that does not book through the trade screens: the moment one passage Item is aboard, the bookings answer and the typed four are ignored.

Manifest lists every cargo and passage Item aboard, with its destination, due day and fare, and the campaign day in the block's header. The hold's used figure is the lots plus the passengers' baggage, so a hold with no lots in it can still read as part full. @UUID[Compendium.mgt2.demo-items.Item.demoCargoLot0001]{Demo — Cargo Lot} and @UUID[Compendium.mgt2.demo-items.Item.demoPassageOutbd]{Demo — Outbound Passage} are worked examples, and the buttons that settle them are on @UUID[Compendium.mgt2.guide.JournalEntry.3wd9e5Iz4A9besSS.JournalEntryPage.HZ0VLzZ4geAh88qk]{Trade}.

Carried craft are bays, each pointing at a whole ship by its Actor UUID, typed in edit mode. A drop will not do it: dropping a spacecraft on this sheet is refused, since a drop here means crew. One row carries a count, so ten fighters on ten clamps are one Actor and one row, and tons is what each costs the hull. The row states what the bay does, and draws a red line if the craft does not fit it (High Guard p.57, p.61). Keep the craft in the world: its purchase price is what comes off the maintenance base, and a ship left in a compendium offers none.

Finance

The figures are the crew's to read; the stored numbers are the referee's, and the server enforces that. Purchase, mortgage override, Benefit quarters and periods paid can be written only by a GM. The last-serviced day stays open to the crew, since the overdue flag depends on it.

  • Purchase is net of any Ship Shares put towards it (Core p.149).
  • Mortgage is the purchase over 240 unless an override says otherwise, which is how a ship bought outright or taken as a Benefit states what it really pays.
  • Maintenance subtracts carried craft from the base (Core p.183). The catalogue's plain division bills a carried boat twice, so where a ship carries craft the Analyses fold shows the difference. This figure takes no override.
  • Life support bills per stateroom, per person awake, and a tenth of that per occupied low berth (Core p.154).
  • Salaries read the crew requirement, not the roster.

Below those come the term, the total repaid, what the loan costs over the price, and what is left. Core p.149 prints the payment and the 40 years and never multiplies them; the sheet counts twelve payments a year, which comes to 480 and to exactly twice the price. The Mortgage billed every four weeks rule counts thirteen instead.

Nothing here bills anyone. No button charges a period, moves a purse or advances the count. You type periods paid. Money is an agreement at your table, and the Finance tab is the arithmetic for it.

The last-serviced day is a campaign day stamp. Leave it empty and the ship is simply unrecorded; a stamp is counted against the campaign day in periods of 28 days, and only the header flag reads it.

The Analyses fold is the referee's. With Benefit quarters above zero it prices Core p.149's two elections side by side, and Apply writes the override, or clears it. On a mortgaged ship it also opens the skip check of Core p.153, made once per new system a crew on the run arrives in. That window seeds the Law Level from the world the voyage says the ship is at, and takes the rest from you. The roll stores the parsecs run and the disguise on the ship for the next arrival, and it tells you whether they are hunted; reset the parsecs to zero yourself when they are discovered.

A robot sheet is a design worksheet and a statblock at once. Most of the thirteen printed lines are computed from a few design choices (Robot Handbook p.13-31), so this sheet does two things no other does: it shows the arithmetic behind its numbers, and it keeps budgets that warn without refusing.

The rule to remember is that a robot's scores are projections. Hits, STR, DEX, END and INT come from the design. Change the design, not the number.

A robot's token is unlinked, because several may be dropped at once and each takes its own damage. A robot played as a Traveller is the exception, and linking its token is yours to do.

The design line

In Edit the header takes the design: Size, TL, Slots removed, Brain, INT bought, Resiliency, Cost and Owner. Size is the spine: one number gives Base Slots, Base Hits, the attack DM, Spaces and the basic cost (Robot Handbook p.13), so the selector shows each row's Slots and Hits.

Cost is typed and nothing writes it. The sheet computes the chassis cost, but a finished robot's price depends on the options, which are free text here.

The readout grid is the statblock. It holds no controls; everything in it is computed or edited somewhere else on the sheet.

Programming names the brain grade, with the highest difficulty it may attempt beneath, when the taskCeiling optional rule is on. A check made by this robot on INT, EDU or SOC shows that ceiling on the roll prompt. It warns and does not block (Robot Handbook p.115).

States

All four are readouts. Wrecked and Destroyed come from the wound, Overload from the Bandwidth budget and Inoperable from radiation, when the rads that reached the brain have taken INT to 0. A robot is never unconscious and never dead.

Budgets

The rail carries two budgets and the brain block a third. Slots and Zero-slot options flag an overrun without the danger colour, because the Robot Handbook gives no penalty for going over: it is a design-time warning. Bandwidth does take the danger colour, since an overloaded brain is a state the rules define.

Slots is the total of the options that cost one, against what the chassis offers. Base Slots is the Size table's figure and never moves, because the book's "per Base Slot" costs and "percentage of Slots" roundings keep using it even after you remove Slots. A robot with no locomotion gets a quarter more available Slots without raising Base Slots.

Zero-slot options count against the Default Suite's allowance, which the info icon works out for this robot. Past it, each further zero-slot option costs a real Slot, and a row appears in the panel above. That coupling is why the two are shown side by side.

Hits

The bar runs to twice the maximum, with two marks, because a robot is wrecked at damage equal to its Hits and irreparably destroyed at twice that (Robot Handbook p.13). Clicking the Hits figure or the broken heart opens the damage dialog, with Repair in place of Heal.

Hits are the Size table's figure plus Resiliency, and there is no field to type them into. To change them, change those two.

Armor shows the Protection of the robot's TL band, unless it carries an Armour trait: that trait is then what prints, and the band's figure is not added. This is what lets a transcribed statblock state the total, and the trait stays the way to do it. A printed Armour (+7, +10 vs. lasers) puts 7 in the figure; the 10 is the robot's reflec, which counts on top of it against a laser (Robot Handbook p.32). The damage card adds it, and hovering the figure shows 17 vs. Laser. An armour Item dropped here gets a row under Armors, with the shield to wear it, the eye to open it and the trash to delete it, and worn it adds to that figure.

Two weapon types behave differently on a robot through the damage card. A Stun weapon meets half the robot's Protection and damages Hits rather than END. An ion weapon meets no armour and shuts the brain down for a number of rounds, reported as a notification, unless the brain is hardened. Radiation is a dose to the brain: see Brain.

Derivations

Three chains written out term by term, so a wrong efficiency flag can be told from a wrong TL band: endurance, speed and chassis cost. A greyed term is at its neutral value. When a figure looks wrong, this block is where to look.

The design fields that feed them are in Edit beneath the chains:

  • Tactical speed is signed, up or down in metres, and each step also moves the endurance.
  • Vehicle Speed Movement replaces metres with a Speed Band altogether, and the statblock then prints the band. A hint gives the endurance while that movement is in use, since the robot keeps its own figure the rest of the time.
  • Agility Enhancement adds to DEX.
  • Power source is the source. RTG or solar running alone halves movement and STR and costs Agility until Second power source is ticked for a second unit (Robot Handbook p.55). A half-life is typed for those sources.
  • Power packs and Efficiency multiply the endurance, and also set END for a Traveller robot.

Exactly one is primary, chosen with the star in Edit, and only that one feeds speed, endurance and chassis cost. Both grant their traits, which print under the Traits block; they count for reading, not as chips you can remove. With no primary marked, the first row answers.

A robot as a Traveller

Biological marks a living body with a robot brain, which vacuum wounds like a Traveller (see @UUID[Compendium.mgt2.guide.JournalEntry.3wd9e5Iz4A9besSS.JournalEntryPage.NXswhOUqMQZKe9lQ]{Regions and hazards}).

Is a Traveller reveals the six characteristics in a block of their own. Nothing else about the type changes (Robot Handbook p.115). Four of them are projections and the block's base fields add to them, so leave those at 0. EDU and SOC are the two you type, because no design field produces them. Society records whether robots are property or citizens here. It is a note for you and writes nothing to SOC (Robot Handbook p.117).

These six can be rolled and they appear on the roll prompt. Without the flag, a check can still use the four projections.

Under this flag the sheet has no Recovery block, careers or finance. A robot is repaired from the damage dialog.

Attacks and skills

Attacks and Weapons split on the weapon Item's Natural flag, as on a creature, and the + makes an ordinary weapon until you tick it. Skills are talent Items and roll as usual; the info icon gives the level cap for a stored skill. A printed skill level can be higher because the characteristic DM is folded in, which matters when transcribing.

Traits are chips in the robot vocabulary. Description and Notes are rich text.

The Attack DM on the statblock comes from Size. It is printed for the attacker to add; no prompt reads it.

A world is an Actor that holds one line of digits and reads everything else from it. Paste a profile and the sheet gives you trade codes, fuel, berthing and both traffic DMs. It is also where the state of a place is kept when it has to outlive any one voyage, such as a supplier who refused the crew last week.

A new world is the referee's and readable by all players, since Core p.238 hands the trade chapter to them. Change that through ownership, as with any Actor.

The profile

The strip holds eight cells: starport, size, atmosphere, hydrographics, population, government, law level and tech level (Core p.248). The cells are the stored data. The printed line is a reading of them. A digit past 9 prints as its letter, and the small text beneath each cell gives the decimal and, where the books name it, the meaning.

In Edit each cell is a field, and Paste a UWP line takes the bare nine characters, such as A788899-C, and fills all eight at once. It accepts exactly that shape: a full catalogue row with the name, hex and trade codes around it is rejected, with a warning, and the field returns to the current line. Pasting replaces the cells once. After that they are edited one by one.

Suppliers

Two facts about a supplier outlast any voyage, so they live on the world rather than on the ship (Core p.241-243):

  • Each search made here this month costs DM-1 on the next one. Record a search stamps the campaign day. Clear searches empties the list. The DM is worked out from those stamps, so no counter needs clearing when a month ends.
  • A trader who refuses a deal cannot deal with that supplier for a month. Walk away records the day, the block prints when the door opens again, and Clear refusal undoes it.

Both read the world setting that holds the campaign day, which you advance yourself; a month is 28 days. If the day never moves, a refusal never expires.

The system works out the trade codes from the profile, and you may overrule any of them. The block prints both readings: Derived is what the digits say and Published is what this world uses, and everything that reads a world reads the published list.

The ledger prints all the codes with the condition behind each, so you can see why one did or did not apply. In Edit each row offers Auto, On and Off. Auto follows the digits and is the normal state. On or Off holds that answer whatever the digits do afterwards, so remember it when you change the profile: the row marks the code as forced.

The override and the condition stay side by side on purpose. A forced code with no condition printed beside it would look like a typo.

What this world is worth

The masthead

The masthead stands above every tab and never scrolls. It holds up to three things.

  • Identity. The portrait, the name and one line of tags: the Tech Level, a skill's level, a weapon's scale. The spine down the side of the sheet reads the sub-type where there is one.
  • The supply cell. Weight, quantity, cost, the Equipped toggle and the storage select, on the types a person carries. A contract puts its terms there instead.
  • The binding. What rolling this item means, written as a sentence. Weapons and talents carry the roll block, and a disease carries the hazard block.

A sheet opens in play mode, where it reads as a record. The toggle in the title bar switches it to edit mode, and closing the sheet puts it back. The mode belongs to that one open window and is stored nowhere.

Some controls stay live in play mode, because they are part of the session rather than of the item's construction: Equipped, the storage select, Reload, the loaded round and a drug's dose button.

Five tabs carry almost everything, and a tab with nothing to show for this document is left out.

An attack of a type it names meets that score in place of Protection, so worn Ablat stops 6 of a laser and 1 of a bullet. Reputation change is the referee's alone. It takes its circumstances from the select beside it, and the best DM applies.

Nearly every check in the system passes through this one window: a characteristic, a skill, a weapon, a psionic talent, a disease, and a ship's or a vehicle's actions. It builds itself from what is being rolled, so a bare characteristic check is short and a ranged attack is long. Each row below appears only where it applies.

The numbers are yours to change until you press a button. Nothing is spent and nothing is written while the window is open.

The readout

The foot of the window is live. It shows the dice and the total DM, the target, every term by name, and a strip of Effect from failure to success with a marker on where the check lands.

That marker assumes a roll of 7, the average of 2D, and the caption says so. A player weighing two options is choosing an Effect, so the Effect comes before the dice. The preview adds up through the same code the roll uses, so the two cannot disagree.

The three buttons

Bane, Roll and Boon each carry the dice they roll: 3D keeping the two lowest, 2D, or 3D keeping the two highest (Core p.61). There is no stacking: a check has a Boon, a Bane or neither. On a request where the referee imposed one, each button states what it would really roll, because a Boon and a Bane cancel to 2D.

Check

The characteristic select lists what this actor can roll, with its current value and DM. A wounded characteristic gives its wounded DM. The blank entry is no characteristic at all.

The skill select starts with two entries that look alike and are not.

  • No skill — characteristic check is a characteristic check (Core p.58). No skill is missing, so the DM is +0.
  • Not proficient is a skill check by someone who lacks the skill, at DM-3 (Core p.59). The prompt reads Jack-of-All-Trades here, reducing the penalty by its level (Core p.69), which is why that skill is never listed as a skill of its own.

A skill the Traveller holds in another speciality is listed at level 0 (Core p.58). A weapon opens on its bound skill, or on Not proficient if it has none. A roll from a characteristic has no skill select.

Chain and Opposed

These two rows exist once the chat log holds a check with an Effect. They read the six most recent you can see, plus anything a card offered through its Chain into control.

Chain applies the task chain of Core p.63: the Effect of an earlier check is a DM on this one, read off the table and never added raw. You may pick several, because working together is that same table read once per contributor. A check already used is marked and still allowed, since the book does not forbid it.

Opposed modifies nothing. The check rolls as normal and its card compares the two Effects (Core p.62). The two rows are independent, so a check can be chained from one roll and opposed by another. An opposed Melee check is a grapple, and its card offers the winner the choices of Core p.78.

Reach

A psionic talent with a reach, on a Traveller whose sheet shows PSI, gets a strip of up to three bands. The first is the printed reach. The others cost double and four times the PSI cost (Core p.229), and the strip states the points. It is a spend and not a DM, so it never touches the formula. The points leave the reserve when the check is rolled, and with no PSI left the prompt refuses to open at all.

Range

A ranged weapon gets this row, and a weapon ticked Melee does not.

Distance is the shot. Type it and the band paints itself beside the field with its DM and the span it covers (Core p.76-77). If exactly one token is targeted and the scene's grid units name the weapon's own unit, the field arrives filled from the canvas, and the band says who it measured to until you type over it. A shot out of range still rolls, with no DM. The band is a warning and the referee rules on it.

The rest of the row holds the common modifiers of Core p.74.

  • Aiming is a ladder of Minor Actions, each worth DM+1. A burst, full auto or a second weapon forfeits it, and the ladder greys out to show that.
  • Fire mode appears on a weapon with Auto. Burst adds the Auto score to damage. Full auto makes that many attacks, posting one card for each. Each states the rounds it costs (Core p.79).
  • Laser sight counts only while aiming.
  • Cover and Prone describe the target.
  • Cross-scale is a declaration that the target is on the other scale (Core p.167). Unticked means the scales match.
  • Fast-moving target takes the target's movement, and buys a DM per full ten metres.
  • Extreme range states the distance past which every shot is Extreme, unless the weapon has Scope and aimed (Core p.77). It opens on the Extreme range beyond optional rule's reading, and you can change it for this shot. A weapon ranged in kilometres is not offered it.

In zero gravity the prompt adds a line stating the Athletics check the shooter owes, or that Zero-G exempts them (Core p.81). It is stated, and rolled by nobody.

Weapon traits

The weapon's traits appear as chips, in three tones, and the tooltip on each says why.

  • Solid is already in the total: Bulky and Very Bulky against the attacker's STR DM, Ramshackle.
  • Pressable is yours to confirm: Inaccurate, Accurate, Spread, Scope, Artillery. A chip whose rule depends on the distance follows the Distance field until you press it, and then stops.
  • Dashed contributes nothing to this roll. AP, Lo-Pen, Blast, Radiation and the like need a target, so they travel with the attack and resolve on the @UUID[Compendium.mgt2.guide.JournalEntry.3wd9e5Iz4A9besSS.JournalEntryPage.Fi5TR1jZrgXracji]{damage card}.

Auto is a chip stating its score, and the fire mode strip is its control. A loaded round's traits are the ones shown.

Modifiers

Every standing source on the actor is listed here by name, already ticked. Untick one to waive it for this roll. That is what waivable means in this system: the referee or the player sees each penalty and can set it aside, and the sheet is not changed.

  • Fatigue, nausea, and the physical-only encumbrance and starvation.
  • Armour worn without the skill it requires (Core p.100).
  • A skill augment (Core p.107).
  • A low-gravity band from a Region, physical checks only.
  • Actor modifier, the sum of whatever Active Effects and the sheet place on checks.
  • Reactions already taken, until they are cleared (Core p.76).

A source whose rule reaches only some checks follows the Check row. Choose STR and the encumbrance tick comes on, choose INT and it goes off, until you touch it yourself.

Situational controls follow them.

  • Dual weapons appears on any attack, at DM-2, and forfeits aiming (Core p.78).
  • Called shot appears on an attack under the Update 2026 vehicle combat rules (Vehicle Handbook p.10).
  • Custom DM is a free number, or a formula such as 1d3. Either goes in the total and is named on the card; the live readout counts only a plain number.
  • Damage sustained appears on a skill check that might be an Extended Action. Enter the damage from the card, not a DM: it becomes the negative DM of Core p.75, and the card then states whether the round's work was kept, lost or ruined.
  • Timeframes is DM+2 for taking longer and DM-2 for rushing, modifying the check rather than the target (Core p.63).

What cannot be waived: a solid trait chip, and anything the referee imposed.

Target

The difficulty ladder shows the target numbers, with the name beside it following the pointer. An item may open it on a rung of its own.

The empty cell means no difficulty was stated. The check is then measured against Average 8+ (Core p.61), and the card says that this was assumed. On a robot, under the robot task ceiling optional rule, a caption says whether the rung is within its brain's reach (RH p.115). It is a caption and not a gate, because outside help can bring a task back within reach.

Visibility chooses who sees the card, among Foundry's four roll modes.

When the referee asked

A check answering a request opens with what @UUID[Compendium.mgt2.guide.JournalEntry.3wd9e5Iz4A9besSS.JournalEntryPage.TUwYdm40vTQJiuSJ]{the Docket} fixed. The fixed rows are static readouts marked GM, and the player cannot change them. An Asked by the referee row at the top carries the reason, any named DM and any stance. If the referee offered several characteristics the select stays, narrowed to those, and the best is chosen first. Modifiers on the player's own side stay waivable.

What pressing a button does

The formula is checked first, so a bad custom DM spends nothing. Then, in order:

  1. A magazine is debited, or the attack refused if it holds too few rounds.
  2. The dice roll and the Effect is scored against the target.
  3. On an Initiative roll, the Effect is written to the combatant, because the Effect is the Initiative (Core p.73).
  4. PSI is spent, for a power.
  5. The card posts. See @UUID[Compendium.mgt2.guide.JournalEntry.3wd9e5Iz4A9besSS.JournalEntryPage.Fi5TR1jZrgXracji]{Chat cards}.

Closing the window instead cancels everything, and any chain offered from a card stays offered.

The switches that change what this window offers are on @UUID[Compendium.mgt2.guide.JournalEntry.3wd9e5Iz4A9besSS.JournalEntryPage.Ca06CCZpxbTWBWGG]{Optional rules}.

Three cards carry the game: the check card, the damage card and the request card. They are built to be read afterwards as well as during, so each states what happened and leaves the decision that is yours as a button.

Nothing on a card reaches into a sheet until somebody presses that button. Cards draw on a light ground whatever the viewer's colour scheme, because Foundry's chat log forces it.

The check card

The head names what was rolled and against what: the difficulty, or no difficulty set.

Under it come the sentences a check resolves to, each only when it applies: the fire mode, the rounds spent, the PSI spent, an Extended Action's verdict, a combat mishap, and an opposed result. The opposed line can be clicked to jump to the check it was measured against.

The dice line shows the formula and the total. Click it to open the dice and every named term, which is where a reader audits the roll. If no difficulty was stated, the terms say the check was assumed at Average 8+, and the Effect is labelled with the number it was measured against.

Then comes the Effect, with its band. The band names are the book's (Core p.61), and the card's colour follows them.

A chained check opens with a strip naming its sources and their total DM. Each source is a link that scrolls the log to it, so a chain can be followed back after the fact. A check answering a request opens with a similar Asked by the referee strip, which links to the request card.

Its buttons

Which buttons appear depends on what was rolled.

  • Roll damages appears wherever the thing rolled has a damage score. With an Effect to carry it reads Roll damage, and says that Effect. It posts the damage card. An attack that missed offers it only if the weapon has Blast, which may still catch someone nearby (Core p.131); that roll adds no Effect. Under the Combat Mishaps rule a double 1 misses whatever the total (Companion p.53).
  • Apply first aid appears on a check made with a first aid skill. It offers the Effect as points, minimum one (Core p.82). Select the patient's token and press. You place the points in a dialog, and the sheet records that first aid was used, refusing a second.
  • Resolve the grapple appears when a Melee check was opposed and not tied. The winner picks the outcome (Core p.78). Any wound it causes posts as an ordinary card with an Apply button.
  • Duration appears on a psionic talent with a duration, and rolls it.
  • Chain into… offers this check to whatever you roll next, and appears only if the world setting turns it on. It is the same chain the prompt's own row offers, made one click shorter.
  • Ask the same is the referee's, also behind a world setting. It opens @UUID[Compendium.mgt2.guide.JournalEntry.3wd9e5Iz4A9besSS.JournalEntryPage.TUwYdm40vTQJiuSJ]{the Docket} already carrying this check.

The damage card

This card names no target on purpose. Attackers do not resolve damage: the defender does. Select the token that was hit and press Apply. That works for anyone who owns the token, and several tokens can be selected for a blast. If nothing you own is selected, a notice says so and nothing is applied.

The card shows three readings of the same attack.

Stored valueMeaning
fullFull
reducedReduced
minimumMinimum

Full is the ordinary one. Reduced and Minimum are the Companion's dice for creatures that take damage differently (Companion p.93), rolled with the attack so that all three are real results. Each reading spells out the dice and the additions, so you can see the Effect survive the change.

When you approach the card, it looks at the selected token. If that token's traits select a reading, the card marks it and moves the pick there, until you pick one by hand. Two tokens that disagree get no mark. An immune defender is marked immune, with the attack void. The pick lives in your own client and is never stored on the message.

With a vehicle selected, a strip of facings appears, because the armour a vehicle meets an attack with depends on the side hit (Core p.140).

The line under the readings lists what the attack carries into the apply step: scale, damage type, AP, Lo-Pen, Destructive, Stun, the Effect, and the Effect 6+ floor.

What Apply does

On each selected token, in order:

  1. An immune defender takes nothing.
  2. The scale ratio applies, when weapon and target differ (Core p.167).
  3. Protection, multiplied by Lo-Pen, comes off, less AP (Core p.77, Core p.79). Worn armour with a second score against the attack's damage type meets it with that score instead (CSC p.18), and a printed Armour trait's second score adds to the first (Robot Handbook p.32).
  4. Under the natural resilience optional rule, the END DM comes off.
  5. A ship's mount multiplies what remains.
  6. An attack at Effect 6+ always does at least one point (Core p.77).
  7. The wound is written: on a person, down the actor's damage chain.

Some attacks then do more, and each reports itself. Stun drains END only, and the excess is rounds of incapacitation (Core p.79). A Radiation weapon delivers a dose, and Poison and Diseased place an Item on the target. Ion weapons have their own handling on robots, vehicles and ships.

The card keeps no record of being applied. A second click is a second wound. It is also how you apply one attack to two targets in turn.

The request card

Posted by @UUID[Compendium.mgt2.guide.JournalEntry.3wd9e5Iz4A9besSS.JournalEntryPage.TUwYdm40vTQJiuSJ]{the Docket}, this card is a live reading of the log. The head states the demand, and the terms state what was imposed. A spread of six cells, one per Effect band, gathers a marker for each answer. One line per Traveller says who is asked and what it costs them, with the skill at its level.

Each line ends in one of three things.

  • A chit, showing the total DM, on a line that is yours to answer. Click it to roll. Shift-click always opens the prompt.
  • The Effect, once answered, which links to the answer.
  • A state: waiting, unclaimed, cannot answer, or declined.

A referee's own rows do not appear on a player's copy at all, and if the referee hid the rung, the player's copy omits it along with the dice totals, since a total minus an Effect is the target. The foot counts the answers, or shows the chain or the sum.

The buttons are Decline for a player, and Conclude, Withdraw and Ask again for the referee. What each does is on @UUID[Compendium.mgt2.guide.JournalEntry.3wd9e5Iz4A9besSS.JournalEntryPage.TUwYdm40vTQJiuSJ]{the Docket}.

Other cards

The same frame carries smaller records, so a day's events can be read back from the log.

  • Recovery cards state a healing procedure and the points placed.
  • Exposure cards state a radiation dose, what the armour stopped, and what it did.
  • Environment cards state what a Region did. See @UUID[Compendium.mgt2.guide.JournalEntry.3wd9e5Iz4A9besSS.JournalEntryPage.NXswhOUqMQZKe9lQ]{Regions and hazards}.
  • Dose cards state a drug's onset, duration and what it leaves. See @UUID[Compendium.mgt2.guide.JournalEntry.3wd9e5Iz4A9besSS.JournalEntryPage.8jfYJ4JuROi9vd17]{Active Effects}.

Trade, passenger and credit cards are described with their screens.

The Docket is how a referee asks the table for a check. You compose one demand, see what it means for each Traveller before anything is sent, and post a single card that everyone answers on. It is referee-only.

Its point is the reading. A name typed in a hurry that resolves to DM-3 for half the party is visible here, on the roster, while it can still be changed.

Opening it

  • The clipboard control beside the chat input opens it. Right-click that control for your last ten demands: picking one posts it straight away at the current roster, with no window.
  • Ask for Initiative, in the combat tracker's menu, opens it seeded with the combatants and a DEX or INT characteristic check.
  • Ask the same, on a check card, opens it carrying that check. A world setting offers the button.
  • An @Request link in any text opens it through the small bubble beside the link.

A macro can reach it as game.mgt2.docket. Opening it seeds the roster from your selected tokens, or failing that from every active player's assigned character.

Composing the demand

Ask says how the skill is named.

  • Named takes a skill you type, suggesting every skill on the roster plus the vehicle skills. A psionic power can be named too.
  • No skill is a characteristic check.
  • Open lets each player pick their own.

The reason is a line printed on the card. The characteristic control means what the number selected means (Core p.59): none lets the player pick, one is fixed, and several are offered for the player to choose among.

Target is the difficulty ladder. Its empty cell is a real answer, and the check is then measured against an assumed Average 8+, recorded on each answer.

Dice is the stance, Boon or Bane or neither, and the timeframe.

DM takes a value and what it is for. A DM with no label is refused, because the book cares where a DM comes from (Core p.64). Ambush names the side that was aware: DM+6 to it and DM-6 to the other (Core p.73). It is offered on a characteristic check only, and Your side means the referee's own rows.

The roster

Who is the list of who answers. Add from the combat, your selected tokens or the party, or drop an Actor on the roster: a Traveller, an NPC or a robot. Adding never replaces, and nobody is added twice.

Each row reads the demand against that one sheet.

  • Answers names the player the line will go to, frozen at posting. A Traveller whose player is offline reads unclaimed and waits; you can still answer for them.
  • Resolves to shows the skill on this sheet: the skill and level, or Not proficient with its penalty, or unresolved here.
  • DM is the total this Traveller will roll at.

Unresolved needs a word. If nobody on the roster has heard of the name, the system will not assume DM-3 for a skill that may not exist under that spelling. The line posts asking the player to pick their own skill. A Traveller with no way to answer, such as a robot asked for a characteristic it lacks, reads cannot answer.

A row has four controls.

  • GM rolls takes the row yourself, whispered (Companion p.7). A creature no player has any stake in starts this way.
  • Override lets this line disagree with the demand: its own skill, characteristics or rung, and who it is opposed by. Pairing two rows makes an opposed check, settled by whichever answers second (Core p.62).
  • Duplicate asks the same Traveller twice, for a rule that wants two checks at different rungs (Companion p.151).
  • Remove takes it off.

Read and Send

The foot gives the demand in plain words, the counts that matter, and a spread: one mark per row on the Effect bands, as an average roll of 7 would land.

Tally decides what the card adds up.

  • Each on their own counts answers, and is the usual choice.
  • Working together is the task chain read once per contributor into one Traveller's final check (Core p.63). On the card you click a line's marker to make that Traveller the resolver. Their prompt opens with the others' answers already chained, and their chit grows as answers land.
  • Σ Effect adds the Effects, for a rule that sums them (Mercenary Book 1 p.47).

Send is Public, or Addressed, which whispers the card to its players and the referee. The world setting decides which it starts on.

Show the rung off prints the card without the difficulty for anyone but you, and without the totals that would give it away.

Roll my side now rolls your own rows the moment you post, whispered. Turn it off and they arrive as chits on your copy instead, which is what you want when an NPC's roll needs the prompt.

One roll for the side, offered on a characteristic check, rolls your side once on its highest score (Core p.73).

Post request sends it, and Enter does too. An empty roster is refused.

Answering

A player clicks the chit on their line. If the demand fixes one characteristic and the skill is resolved, that one click rolls, with every standing modifier applied as the prompt would have it, and no window. Otherwise the prompt opens with the fixed parts locked; see @UUID[Compendium.mgt2.guide.JournalEntry.3wd9e5Iz4A9besSS.JournalEntryPage.AFpVHfj7ijV7S9ct]{the roll prompt}. A power always opens the prompt, because reach is a spend. Shift-click always opens it.

The answer is an ordinary check card, marked as asked for. Decline posts a line saying that Traveller is not making the check, and needs no permission of any kind.

Each player chooses, in a client setting, what arriving does on their own screen: flash the card, open the roll, or nothing. Flashing never scrolls the log, and nothing is rolled for them.

Concluding

Nothing concludes on its own. Conclude can be pressed at any time and lights up once nobody is waiting, and the choice stays yours, because deciding what the results mean is the referee's job.

  • Conclude freezes the card as a record: its lines, its Effects and its total. A later answer is still a check in the log, and reads as late. A second answer to an open line counts as superseded, and the first stands.
  • Withdraw closes the request. Answers already made stand as the checks they are.
  • Ask again posts the same demand to the same roster as a new card, leaving the first in the log. The book prints no reroll, so a retry is a second, honest record. A world setting offers the button.

Writing a request into text

Any text Foundry enriches, such as a journal or an adventure, can carry a demand. Write these three parts in one run, with no spaces between them: @Request, then the demand in square brackets, then the link's text in braces if you want one.

  • {Spot the breach}

The bubble beside it, shown to the referee only, opens the Docket on that demand. Text is not a referee: a demand becomes one only when you post it.

Traveller creation is a group activity. The book says so (Core p.8), and its Connections Rule depends on it. The system runs it as one window the table shares: a grid with one column per Traveller and one row per term.

No session document stands behind that grid. An Actor is on the roster because it carries a creation ledger, so a table can stop in the middle of a term, close Foundry and come back a week later by opening the window. Everything creation decides is written to the Traveller as it is decided: the skills, the contacts, the career record and its term log. The ledger holds only what is still pending, and it is thrown away when creation finishes.

One career Item holds a whole printed career: its qualification line, its assignments with their Survival and Advancement checks, its rank ladders, its skill tables, its Events and Mishaps, and its two Benefit columns. @UUID[Compendium.mgt2.guide.JournalEntry.3wd9e5Iz4A9besSS.JournalEntryPage.Kxn4HoBIv7mHLlDx]{Item sheets} says how each part is filled in. A gap in a career is not an error. An assignment with no Survival number runs a term with no Survival check. A career with no Events table says so and moves on. A Benefit column left out makes the closing screen ask the referee for the row.

Three behaviours catch people out.

  • The Traveller gets a copy. Dropping a career on a sheet copies the template whole into a record. Editing the template afterwards changes no record already on a Traveller.
  • A name is the key. A draft row, a compelled career and a sub-table all name their target in text, with case and punctuation folded. The search looks at the world first, then every Item compendium.
  • Skills are not fetched. A grant matches the Traveller's own skills and otherwise creates one under the name the row prints. It never copies a skill Item out of a library, so print the name you want on the sheet. The speciality is part of the match, whether it sits in the skill's field or only in its name: a bare Gun Combat grant leaves a held Gun Combat (slug) alone and creates the bare skill beside it.

The table's terms

Set the Character creation page of @UUID[Compendium.mgt2.guide.JournalEntry.3wd9e5Iz4A9besSS.JournalEntryPage.Ca06CCZpxbTWBWGG]{Optional rules} before anyone rolls. It decides how characteristics are assigned, whether boon dice apply, and whether Iron Man, a cap on terms, picked skills or solo generation are in force. The grid's masthead states the assignment method and everything that differs from the printed game, so the players can read the terms before they start.

The Psionic Strength chip exists only where the Psionics rule is on, which stands in for the referee's permission Core p.228 asks for.

The window

Three doors open it. The Actor directory has a Character creation button in its header, and that is how you resume with nobody selected. A Traveller's entry in the directory and the menu on their sheet both offer Add to character creation. The sheet of a blank Traveller, or of one in creation, also carries a strip with a button to start or resume, shown to its owner. Dragging a Traveller onto the foot of the grid does the same thing, and that is how a player brings their own.

The window has four blocks.

The masthead gives the term the table has reached, read off the furthest column, then how many are still serving and the table's terms. It holds the button for connections and the door to mustering out.

The grid has a column per Traveller. The head shows the name, the species and the age, and clicking a column selects it. A cell shows the career, the assignment and each thing that term did. The tail is ragged on purpose: a Traveller who has stopped has no cell where the others still have one, and their head carries how they left. That badge opens the closing screen.

The cross on a column takes the Traveller off the roster. Everything already decided stays on them; only the ledger goes. See Finishing below for what this does not do.

The strip is the term's only control, and it reads the selected column's frame. Steps the frame adds are marked, steps it cuts are struck through, and it prints the frame's reason and its source.

The tray shows what the selected Traveller has pending, and their two counters.

Selecting a column is per client, so players each watch their own. Only a user who can edit a Traveller runs their steps: the owner rolls. Reopening a step and editing the tray belong to the referee.

Before the first term

Three chips stand before the numbered steps, because they run once and not once a term. Take them in this order, since the second reads what the first produced.

Characteristics (Core p.9). The chip rolls what the frame declares and posts one card with every die, then a dialog assigns the results. The rule How rolled numbers reach characteristics decides the shape: in printed order nothing is chosen, otherwise each picker holds a distinct result and changing one swaps the two. A slot on a species' own dice keeps its roll, and a fixed value is written as printed. The scores are stored as rolled, and every later change is a row of the Traveller's characteristic log. Pressing the chip again asks first.

Background skills (Core p.9). The allowance is EDU DM + 3, read at that moment with the species' modifier included. A frame may print its own count or its own dice. The list comes from the frame, otherwise from the linked Background Skills table, and it is an offer rather than a fence: a player may type a skill it does not list. A pick of a skill already held buys nothing, and the step reports it as unspent.

Psionic Strength (Core p.228). The first press tests. Above 0 the chip then opens the training window, and at 0 it has nothing left to do.

The term

A term needs a career on the Traveller. Drag the career to their sheet, not to the grid, which refuses it and says where it belongs. A Traveller holds one open career at a time, and a record never entered gives way to the new one.

The step in progress is highlighted, and running a step moves to the next. Any step can be pressed at any moment, so the order is the table's discipline and not a lock. Each step runs once a term. If a step has to run again, the referee reopens it from the strip: what it wrote stays, and only its own verdict is cleared.

The Core sequence (Core p.18-20) runs as follows.

Start-of-term elections. Anagathics, begun, kept up or stopped (Core p.49). Beginning makes the roll that book prints, and on that roll an exact 2 compels the Traveller into a career that opens only by force. A term on them costs money out of the eventual benefits and means two Survival checks. Stopping for any reason forces an ageing roll at once.

Qualification. Continuing a career is no roll. To enter one, the player picks an assignment first, so closing the picker rolls nothing, and then the roll is composed from the career's own line: previous careers, age, conditional DMs and any tray entry that bears on it. A career may instead let the Traveller in automatically above a score, or only with the referee's leave. Leave is tested first, so a player without it is refused, whatever their score. A referee needs none. A career that opens only by force admits a referee and refuses a player. Entering pays rank 0's bonus at once. The Traveller cannot return to the career just left unless it is always open, and an ageing crisis fails every qualification and refuses an event's career offer too. Only a forced entry, such as the Prisoner's, still goes (Core p.49). A career whose line reads PSI alone is shut to a Traveller who has lost their psionic abilities.

Basic training. Once per career. The first career trains every skill on the table it names for this at level 0, and that replaces the term's skill roll. A later career trains one skill of the player's choice, and the interpretation Basic training after the first career is additional says whether the term's roll is kept beside it.

Skill roll. The term's own roll, before Survival (Core p.18). Pick a table, then roll 1D. Tables the Traveller may not use are not offered: an officer table without a commission, or a table gated on a score. A roll earned later in the term, by Advancement or by a row, is taken when it is earned: the cursor goes back to this step while the counter holds one. It is the one step that can be pressed repeatedly, once for each roll the counter holds. The two limits of Core p.18 hold throughout. A level past the ceiling is lost, and past the total for INT and EDU a grant degrades as the interpretation A skill grant past the cap degrades to level 0 says.

Survival. A natural 2 always fails. A failure rolls on the career's Mishaps, unless Iron Man is on, when it kills the Traveller and ends the term. A failed Survival loses the term's Benefit roll even where the row does not eject, unless the row gives it back.

Event. 2D on the career's Events. A 7 goes to the linked Life Events unless the career says it owns that row. A row is data and may do a good deal: show text, test a gate, ask a question, throw its own check, grant skills, leave tray entries, offer or compel a career, stake Benefit rolls, or send on to another table. A chain of tables stops at the tenth, or at any table it has already rolled, and says so.

Commission. Only where the career prints one and the record is not already an officer. It is optional, so it asks. The two gates of Core p.19 apply: a first-term limit unless the Traveller's SOC is high enough, and a DM for every later term. The player may lend held Advancement DMs to it. A commission moves the record onto the officer ladder, and that term has no Advancement roll.

Advancement. One roll, three readings (Core p.18). A pass is the next rank, its ladder bonus and an extra skill roll, which the cursor goes back to Skill roll to spend. A total at or under the terms served forces the Traveller out at the end of the term. A natural 12 obliges them to stay. A career left by its own track, such as a prison term, measures the roll against that track instead.

Ageing. From the fourth term by default, or as the frame's own law says, a roll with a DM for terms served (Core p.48-49). The player chooses which characteristics take the loss, each one distinct, and closing the dialog does not cancel it. A score at 0 is a crisis, and the loop only announces it. The care is a row added on the sheet's Health tab. The crisis stands after the care, because the loss is still in the log, and it keeps failing qualification rolls. @UUID[Compendium.mgt2.demo-actors.Actor.demoCharHesperLd]{Demo — Hesper Lund} shows the whole sequence.

PSI is the exception. Aged to 0 it is no crisis, but the Traveller loses every psionic ability and can never regain them (Aliens of Charted Space 1 p.275). The term log and a notice say so. From then on their talents refuse to roll and leave the prompt's skill list, the training window has nothing to offer, a grant of PSI is refused, and a career whose line reads PSI alone is shut.

Continue or leave. The step that closes the term, and the only one that moves the clock. It offers to stay, to change assignment, or to leave. An ejection or a release closes the term with no question, and a natural 12 stays the same way. A forced-out Traveller, one at the cap on terms and one compelled elsewhere can only leave, and a sentence the Advancement roll has not ended can only be continued. If earlier steps were never run, the dialog lists them, because closing the term buys its years and its Benefit roll either way.

Closing the term logs its years, credits the Benefit roll it earned, moves the column to the next term and expires whatever the ending expires. Age is summed from the term log and never worked out from the term number, so a species' own term length and a term that does not age both read true.

A frame's own steps have no procedure in the system. A step with a declared check rolls it and applies what the frame says. One with none tells the referee it is theirs to run.

Refused, drafted, compelled

A failed qualification deletes the career from the sheet, because it was never entered, and the ledger keeps the refusal. The term is not lost. A dialog offers the draft, a career always open, or deciding later, and pressing Qualification with no career brings it back.

The draft (Core p.19) is once in a lifetime, and the interpretation An event-forced draft has its own budget decides whether an event's draft counts against it. With the Draft table linked, 1D picks a row and the Traveller enters that career at once with no roll, past every door it keeps. A career named on the row but held nowhere is reported, and it enters as drafted when someone drops it on the Traveller. With no table linked, the referee types a career.

A career always open is found by its field, in the world and in every Item compendium except the demo packs. Once refused this term, a Traveller can enter nothing else. Another career dropped on the sheet is accepted, and pressing Qualification refuses it and deletes it.

A compelled career comes from an event row or from the anagathics roll and waits on the tray. Until it is entered every other career refuses the Traveller, and the career they are in closes at the end of the term as barred from continuing. A compulsion that names a career nobody holds is dropped, and both the owner and the referee are told.

A mishap that ejects costs the term's Event, Commission and Advancement, and its Benefit roll. The Traveller still serves the term out: Continue or leave closes it with its years. The term's skill roll comes before Survival, so it is already taken. Where a frame puts it after Survival, the interpretation An ejected Traveller still takes the term's skill roll decides that step.

Education

A career of kind Pre-career education goes on the sheet like any other and runs the same strip with a different meaning (Core p.16-17). Connections

Two Travellers agree that an event of one involved the other, and each takes a skill for it (Core p.19). The masthead's button opens the agreement: the pair, a skill for each, and the shared event in your own words. A refusal says which limit it hit and reopens on what was typed.

The system holds the printed limits: two connections per Traveller, each with a different partner, no skill above level 3, and never Jack-of-All-Trades. Both Travellers are written, so whoever presses Agree must be able to edit both. In practice the referee does it. Solo generation removes the rule.

Mustering out

The closing screen opens from the masthead or from a stopped column's badge, and it reads the same roster. It lists each Traveller's service, the Benefit rolls owed, their Cash count, their pension and what they have taken. A Traveller between careers can roll for the career just closed, since benefits come on leaving (Core p.46).

Rolling a Benefit asks which career and which column. Rolls owed are the ledger plus the rank bonus, read against the highest rank reached, so a demotion does not cost it. Cash is limited across the Traveller's whole life and the column closes when the limit is reached. The roll takes Gambler on Cash, the rank's DM and any tray entry; with two or more one-shot DMs waiting, the player picks which ones ride on this roll.

The career's own column decides the outcome. Cash goes to the Traveller's purse. A skill, a characteristic, a contact or a Benefit applies at once, and SOC past the ceiling becomes Ship Shares (Core p.47). A Benefit the Traveller holds and must re-roll gives the roll back. Where the career carries no column, the referee reads the amount or the row out of the book. Cancelling spends nothing, though the dice stay in the log.

Vouchers. A weapon, an armour or an augment is a right with a credit and TL ceiling, not an Item. The check mark on an open one opens a window over the compendiums, filtered by those ceilings, dearest first, and it can be settled by hand instead. It can wait: vouchers stay on the Traveller's sheet after creation.

One ship between the table (Core p.48). Only one Traveller starts the campaign owning a ship. Electing a keeper writes every holder at once, so it needs someone who can edit them all, and the others take a yearly sum per ship rolled. Each Traveller then says how many Ship Shares go towards the ship kept, since the rest pay a yearly sum too.

The shared skills package (Core p.50). No package ships, so the referee types the one the book prints, a comma between entries and a trailing number for a level. Travellers then take turns: whoever has taken fewest is up, and the tally on screen shows why. An interrupted draft resumes where it stood. Solo generation replaces all this with one skill at level 1 and removes the ship election too.

Finishing

Finish ends creation for one Traveller, and Finish creation does it for the whole roster at once, for a user who can edit every column. The confirmation lists what would be lost: a career still being served, Benefit rolls untaken, a ship not settled, package skills left.

Finishing banks the pension, pays debt out of the Traveller's Cash as far as it reaches (Core p.52), writes the age, and removes the ledger. An age the system wrote before is brought up to date, and an age somebody typed stays as it is. The pending tray, both counters and the package picks are discarded. The term log, the career records, the skills and the characteristic log all stay.

Taking a Traveller off the roster with the cross removes the same ledger and does none of that. The pension is not banked and the debt is not paid.

Under Iron Man a dead Traveller's steps refuse, and the career they died in pays no Benefit. The sheet stays. What becomes of it is the referee's decision, and the system never deletes it.

Space combat is its own kind of encounter, with its own window. Position in Traveller is not a map: there is one range band per pair of ships (Core p.165), and that band is the state the screen keeps. A round is three named steps, and every ship takes a step before any ship takes the next (Core p.164). The screen is a board for all of that. It tracks where everyone is and what they have spent, it rolls the checks you press, and it leaves the rulings to you.

Everything the screen shows of a ship comes from its sheet, so build the ship first: @UUID[Compendium.mgt2.guide.JournalEntry.3wd9e5Iz4A9besSS.JournalEntryPage.IQl36fl0PKjut4bg]{Spacecraft}.

Starting a fight

In the combat tracker, open the encounter menu and choose New space combat. It creates the encounter, makes it the active one and opens the screen. Space combat screen in the same menu reopens it. Players have no encounter menu: they right-click a row in the tracker for the same entry. They can read the screen and roll the stations of a ship they own, and everything else on it is the referee's.

Drop a spacecraft on a range band to bring it in. The first one has nothing to be measured against; the next sets its range to the ship the strip is reading from. Dropping a ship that is already in the fight on a band moves it there instead.

A ship joins as one row in the order, with one crew member per station on its roster. Anyone with a linked sheet comes with it. Everyone starts as a Passenger, because the book has the referee assign duties as the battle begins (Core p.164) and a station's name is not a duty.

The trash control on a ship's panel takes it out of the fight, with its crew and every range it was half of.

The range strip

The strip across the top is read from the ship selected in the order, outward. Each other ship is pinned on the band it stands at relative to that ship, and the seven cells carry what each band is worth: the attack DM and the Thrust a change out of it costs. Adjacent and Close print a dash for the DM because the book prints none (Core p.167). A dash is not a zero; those bands resolve as a dogfight.

On a space scene

The band is the truth and a scene is optional. Tables that want tokens on a canvas can have them.

Right-click a scene in the Scenes directory and choose Configure for space combat. It asks first, then makes the scene gridless and measured in kilometres, adds four Levels, one per scale (Contact, Approach, Engagement, Theatre), and adds two Regions: reach the outer edge flying and you are offered the next scale out, reach the centre and you are offered the next one in. It creates no art and no drawings, and it can be run again safely.

On such a scene the token ruler reads a band and a distance instead of grid units. It refuses a path that crosses Levels or changes elevation, since the Levels are drawn at different scales.

For the referee, the token controls gain Set the range band from two tokens. Select exactly two tokens on the same Level, and it measures centre to centre and writes that band to their two ships. It works in one direction only: a measurement becomes a band, and a stored band never moves a token. A ship dropped on the strip joins by its Actor, with no token, so the tool finds it by the token's Actor. Where one Actor flies in two ships or fleets of the encounter it cannot say which, and refuses; read the ruler and click the cell instead.

A round

The left rail holds the round number, the step and the order. Choosing a step is yours; the system does not walk you through them. Ships sort by Initiative, and each row has a pip per step for you to tick as that ship finishes it. The pips are your own marks and enforce nothing, the same way the tracker's turn pointer does.

Initiative is rolled per ship, from the figure at the head of its row, and everyone aboard acts on that number. The formula is printed in the rail: 2D plus the Pilot skill of whoever holds the pilot duty, plus current Thrust, plus any standing DM, plus the Effect of the commander's Tactics (naval) check (Core p.165). That Effect is typed in the rail, because it comes from a check made outside the screen. If nobody holds the pilot duty, the ship's standing pilot answers.

End round does the bookkeeping for every ship at once:

  • Each ship's movement is banked and its allocations are cleared.
  • A pair that has paid for a change moves one band, once, however many ships paid.
  • Every step pip, action tick and reaction clears.
  • The step returns to Manoeuvre.

The Captain's Leadership Effect for next round, and anything else the book times to a round, is yours to remember.

Thrust and closing

Only an owner of the ship sees these blocks, and only the referee can write to them.

Thrust is the pilot's allocation for the round (Core p.165). Add a row per use, name it and give it points. The book prints no closed list of manoeuvres, so a row is whatever the pilot called it, and only rows with the movement box ticked buy range. Docking and aiding gunners do not. Going over the ship's Thrust reads red and is not refused. What is left unallocated shows in the rail as Unspent thrust, which is what evasive action spends (Core p.171).

Closing is the bank (Core p.166). Say which ship this one is manoeuvring against and which band it wants, and the gauge shows what is banked against the cost of leaving the present band. Rows flagged as movement pay into the bank at End round. When two ships name each other, their movement adds if both are closing or both opening, and subtracts if one is running from the other. The bank carries from round to round, and it is typed, so a chase joined part way through can start with what it already has.

Missiles

A salvo is everything one ship fires at one target in one round (Core p.172), and it is tracked as its own contact with an age.

The referee's launch row appears for a ship with a mounted missile. Choose the missile, the target and how many, and Fire. The band between the two ships fixes the flight time, read from where it was fired and not from where the ships are later; with no band set it flies as if from Medium. Firing does not touch the mount's ammo count.

A row then shows what is left of the flight and how many rounds it has to run. Type an Effect beside it and press:

  • Electronic warfare removes that many missiles. A salvo takes one such attempt a round, however many operators try (Core p.173), and the button goes dead for the rest of the round.
  • Point defence removes that many missiles (Core p.171).
  • Impact is live once the salvo is arriving. It rolls the attack: 2D plus the missiles left, against 8+, with neither gunner nor range as a modifier, and DM−2 for a salvo fired at Distant (Core p.173). On a hit the card offers damage for one missile, multiplied by the Effect after armour, and capped at the missiles left.

The Effect you type comes from the check the sensor operator or gunner has already rolled on their station; the screen does not link the two.

A salvo stays on the board after its impact until you remove it. Ten rounds in flight marks it out of fuel and does nothing else (Core p.172). A Smart missile's bonus is stated on the card for you to add, and a salvo launched at Adjacent or Close loses it.

Two optional rules add to this. Dogfight and interceptor missiles adds a class to the launch row with a band each class may not be fired past, which is refused, and a DM at impact (Companion p.167). Staged missile defence adds a layer select to each row: on Area or Point defence the number you type is hits, and the screen rolls a die per hit wherever that layer has a kill number; on Close-in it works as plain point defence (Companion p.168).

What the screen leaves to you

  • Which ship a gunner is aiming at, and every range or size DM that follows from it.
  • Criticals. An Effect of 6 or more is on the card, and the location roll and the Apply button are on the ship's sheet.
  • Ammunition. Nothing counts rounds.
  • Boarding, escape and surrender.
