High Guard offers a second way to fight in space (High Guard p.105-124), for when dozens or hundreds of ships are on the table. It replaces the Core rules for that battle rather than adjusting them, and the system treats it the same way: a separate kind of encounter, with its own screen and its own arithmetic. Three things set it apart from @UUID[Compendium.mgt2.guide.JournalEntry.3wd9e5Iz4A9besSS.JournalEntryPage.A0nyxKJrXcmaX0P8]{Space combat}:

  • Ships move as fleets. Range is measured between fleets, not between hulls.
  • Attacks are not rolled. A shot resolves to a factor and a figure, with no dice. Only a spinal mount rolls to hit.
  • Every figure is the ordinary one divided by 3.5, the mean of 1D, because this is standard space combat with the dice taken out (High Guard p.111).

The two switches

Fleet battles are off by default, and the menu entry is hidden while they are. Turn on Fleet battles in the @UUID[Compendium.mgt2.guide.JournalEntry.3wd9e5Iz4A9besSS.JournalEntryPage.Ca06CCZpxbTWBWGG]{optional rules}. Every spacecraft then gains its Fleet ship sheet tab, and the combat tracker's encounter menu offers New fleet battle.

Fleet manoeuvre chart is a second switch behind the first, and it adds the optional map of High Guard p.122-124.

Turning the first switch off with a battle running does not delete it. The screen opens, says the rule is off, and refuses to add or fire anything. Ships keep their typed Crew Skill either way.

Getting a ship ready

Before a battle, each ship's tab on its sheet should read true, and that comes from three places on the sheet:

  • Crew skill, typed in the Crew block. It is typed and never averaged (High Guard p.110), and a roster of stations could not answer it anyway.
  • Mounts with weapons in them. The tab lists batteries: identical mounts gather onto one line, as the book prints them. A mount that only names a weapon in its label reads 0/N, which is the one figure on the tab that is wrong rather than empty, though its salvo defences are right. Ortillery is left out, missiles read as a salvo, and ion weapons have their own door.
  • Software and Traits. Fire Control, Evade, Launch Solution and Auto-Repair come from the rating of a component of category Software, found by name. The five ship Traits are read off the names of a ship's components too. Both read what is fitted, whether or not it is started.

Setting the battle up

New fleet battle creates the encounter and opens the screen. Add a fleet for each side, then drop spacecraft from the Actors directory:

  • on a fleet's list, a hull joins the line, and a new fleet's hint Drop a spacecraft here to add it to the line stands for the list until a row gives it height;
  • on the Drop a fighter class here line under it, the ship joins as a wing of one, and its number is set in the panel, because a drag cannot carry a number.

One drop is one hull, and the same Actor can be dropped as often as the fleet has ships of that class. Only the referee can add to a battle. A player who owns a fleet's group can, however, run that fleet's command block and panels.

The strip across the top works as it does for ships, one level up: the pins are fleets, clicking a pin picks the fleet being measured, and clicking a cell sets the band between the pair. A fleet's internal spacing is something else, and it lives in Formation.

A round

The three steps carry the Core's names and none of its content. Next step walks them, and pressing it past Actions ends the round; End round does so from anywhere. When a round ends, every fleet's movement is banked, a pair that has paid for a change moves one band, each pool refills, the Morale figure clears, and dispersals tick down.

Initiative has two printed procedures, and they are alternatives (High Guard p.115). Click the number in a fleet's block for one roll for the whole fleet, which every member reads back. Press Per ship to clear that number and roll each hull and wing separately. The block names the procedure in force and prints the formula. A salvo has no Initiative of its own.

The command block

Everything here belongs to the fleet and to no ship in it, for the one fleet selected.

  • Flag ship is set from a ship's panel, and only a hull with a command bridge may fly it (High Guard p.105). It is worth DM+1 on Morale while it survives.
  • Tactics (naval) is the Effect of the commander's check, typed. It joins Initiative.
  • Formation is the fleet's own spacing, not the range to the enemy (High Guard p.117). Adjacent or Close gives every ship Defensive DM+1, Short is the plane of battle, and anything wider counts as dispersing. The line beside it counts the rounds spent out there and says when the one round's grace is gone. It enforces nothing.
  • Thrust is the slowest ship of the line. High Guard p.115 uses "the fleet's Thrust score" and never defines it, so this is the system's ruling, and the box under it replaces it with whatever you type. Reserve ships do not slow the line, and wings have their own.
  • Celestial terrain says this fleet is holding a planet as an obstruction, worth Defensive DM+1 per point of Thrust superiority (High Guard p.124).
  • Breaking off costs Defensive DM−1 and locks spinal mounts (High Guard p.122).
  • Dispersal takes the Effect of the Leadership and Tactics (naval) chain and reads the Fleet Dispersal table: how many rounds it runs and the DM meanwhile, on the Offensive and Defensive DMs alike (High Guard p.122). While it runs the ships take no other action, which is p.115's own name for the Actions Step: Repair and Breaking off refuse. They still fire, which is why the table charges an Offensive DM. Page 122 also prints Morale under that step, but it says the check must be made each round, so this system keeps it open. A failed dispersal charges its two rounds and divides nothing: the ships may try again, and the box says so until one succeeds.

Below that sit the closing controls, the same ones the space combat screen has. Name the fleet and the band, allocate Thrust to movement, and watch the bank fill.

Morale lists its DMs off the battle itself: flag ships, and losses on both sides. Roll morale posts the check. With more than two fleets in the battle it first asks which one opposes this fleet, because the two opposing rows read that fleet's losses and flag ship. The answer stays on this screen until it closes: the rows read it, and so does the Celestial terrain figure in the command block. A shot's own terrain term always reads the fleet firing it. The book prints no target and no consequence, only that Crew Skill may change for that round (High Guard p.122), so nothing is written. The figure you type in Crew skill this round is what moves every ship and wing of the fleet, and it clears at the end of the round.

A ship in the panel

Select a hull in a fleet's list. The panel shows the Fleet Ship Sheet as it stands this round: Crew Skill now over Crew Skill typed, the two Offensive DMs, the Defensive DM alone and against the current target, Armour, Thrust, Jump, the critical thresholds passed.

Its buttons fly or strike the flag, move the ship to the reserve or back to the line (High Guard p.117), and detach it.

Defences are five pools, spent per round and restored when it turns over. Type points and press Spend, or let the attack block below spend them. A pool will not go below zero. The sandcaster pool is sized against whoever is shooting, so it reads the current target.

Radiation exposures count per battle on this hull, not on the ship. Each one takes Crew Skill and a share of the salvo defences down the ladder of High Guard p.121, and the last disables the crew.

Repair appears under any critical the ship is carrying, and spends one Repair Point to take one severity off that location (High Guard p.121). That change is written on the ship.

A wing shows fewer figures. It starts from its full Crew Skill where a ship starts from half, it may have a skill of its own typed in, it loses a fighter for each fighter's worth of Hull, and it has no pools at all (High Guard p.114).

Firing

The book has every target and battery declared before any of them fire (High Guard p.117). The screen follows that: nothing is applied until you say so.

  1. Select the firing contact and pick a target from the opposing fleets.
  2. Tick what the weapon's name would tell a reader: Meson, Fusion or railgun bay, High yield or intense focus. These are ticked, never guessed, because a name cannot be matched in every language. They stay ticked until you change them.
  3. Set how many of the battery fire, and press Fire.

The card shows the Attack Factor, the multiple it reads off the Attack Effectiveness table, and the damage, with its arithmetic. A weapon that cannot reach the band is refused. A weapon whose Damage is at most half the target's Armour reads impervious and deals nothing (High Guard p.118).

A spinal mount reads Roll to hit instead. It is the one attack that rolls, on an Average (8+) check at the ship's Crew Skill, and it refuses a target too small to track.

An ion weapon posts what the target loses and for how long (High Guard p.111-112). Nothing is written, so a ship's lost Thrust or weapons are yours to rule, and a Hardened target ignores it.

The result lands in the Resolved block. There, pick a screen or sandcaster pool and the points to spend, then press Apply. The points come out of the target's own pool and reduce the figure first; then the damage is written.

Applied damage is converted back and taken off the ship's own Hull, and it stays there after the battle. Crossing a tenth of the adjusted pool scores a critical, a further one is added when the attacker is offensively superior, and a big hull ignores those from small mounts (High Guard p.119). Unlike the space combat screen, this path rolls the location and writes the severity itself, and the Resolved block lists each one.

The Resolved block belongs to your client and to the moment: selecting another contact discards an attack you have not applied.

Leaving the battle

Detach sends one hull out of the fleet and into a new space combat of its own, and opens that screen (High Guard p.122). It suits a handful of ships with the Travellers aboard. Each press makes a separate encounter. A dispersal holds it as it holds Split, below.

To divide a fleet, tick what leaves in the command block, under the Dispersal box, and press Split into a new fleet. The ticked hulls and wings become a fleet of this battle with the parent's ranges and none to the fleet they left, and the screen follows them. Fold into a named fleet is the reassembly: this fleet's contacts join that one, and this fleet leaves the battle with its ranges. It confirms first, naming both fleets and the hulls, and it offers every other fleet, the enemy's included, because a fleet records no side. Split and Fold both wait while the box counts rounds, because the ships divide after them (High Guard p.122), and Split and Detach wait on a failed dispersal until one has succeeded. Page 122 asks for the chain before either, and this system does not: neither button asks whether it was rolled.

The manoeuvre chart

With Fleet manoeuvre chart on, a link at the top of the screen opens the chart, and a right-click on a tracker row does too. It is eight rings around a fixed point, each a range band, cut into quadrants and sectors, with each position coded as the book abbreviates it (High Guard p.124).

Pick a fleet, a wing or a salvo from the list and click a cell. A hull is not placed, because a fleet's ships move as a unit. Placing a fleet writes the range to every other placed fleet, into the same band map the strip shows, and the side list prints each pair. Wings and salvoes are marked on the chart and write no range.

The chart is a second writer for one map. A band you set on the strip stands until the next fleet placement rewrites it, and turning the chart off leaves every band where it is.

Trade at a stop is two windows, because the book has two jobs in it (Core p.238-243). Traffic at the stop deals with a route: who wants carrying from here to there. Speculative trade deals with a market: what can be bought and sold at this one counter. Both sit in the token controls, for every user, because the chapter is written for the Travellers to run. A referee is still needed for anything that moves money.

Neither window needs a document. Type a world's profile, such as A788899-C, and every DM on the page works. A travel zone can ride on the end of the line as A or R, which is how a sector table prints it. Dropped Actors are what add the writing:

  • a world fills the profile and zone for you, and gives the window something to remember with;
  • a ship gives the window a hold to fill and purses to reach.

A dropped world fills the fields and does not lock them. Nothing you type there is saved, and closing the window forgets the stop.

Traffic at the stop

Open it, then give it both ends of the route, the parsecs between them, and the ship if you mean to book. A world on the Destination slot is stored on each booking as a link with its name beside it, so the booking still reads if the world is later deleted.

The first block scores both ends twice, once for passengers and once for freight, line by line, and totals each column (Core p.239-240). Cells where the two columns disagree are underlined, which is where a table read by hand usually goes wrong. Below it are the three things on offer.

The leading check. Choose the skill, type the skill-and-characteristic DM, and press the die, or type an Effect you rolled elsewhere. It is a bare Average (8+) roll with your DM, with no roll prompt and no card. The Effect leads the passenger rows, and the freight rows too unless the skill is Carouse, which finds passengers only. Best Steward adds to passengers as well.

Roll all eight rolls the seven traffic checks and mail in one press, and the rows fill in: dice, total, how many dice the table hands back, and what they came to.

  • Passengers are four rows, one per class. The count cannot exceed the world's people (Core p.239), and a capped row says so.
  • Freight is three rows, and each lot rolls its own tonnage, so a row lists every lot and names the biggest. A lot cannot be broken up (Core p.241).
  • Mail is pass or fail against 12+, with a DM banded off the freight total and the armed, rank and SOC boxes from the form. It is all the containers or none.

Post to chat puts the offer on the log with nothing left to press. Pressing Roll all eight again is a new offer, and whatever was booked from the old one comes back on sale.

Booking

The Booking block takes the offer aboard, and it is the referee's: it needs a GM, a ship in the slot, and a named destination. Each line gives its reason when it is not ready.

  • Passengers are booked per class, as many as you enter up to what is on offer. The fare is taken now (Core p.239): the Credit transfer window opens to pay it into the crew's purses, and a passage Item lands on the ship when you confirm. Cancel the transfer and nothing is booked.
  • Freight is taken lot by lot, and Mail whole. No money moves. Each is a cargo Item carrying its fare, paid on delivery (Core p.241).

Fares come from the parsecs. Over-full berths and a hold too small are warned about and never refused: a shortage is the crew's to solve. Baggage comes out of the hold too, so a booking can tip a hold over with no lot added.

Due in (days) is your number, since the chapter prints no deadline. It stamps a lot with the campaign day it falls due. Leave it blank for no deadline: such a lot can never be late, and its card names no day.

Delivery

A booking ends at the far end, on the ship's own Manifest block, because that is the document that made the trip. A GM is needed for both buttons.

Deliver hands a freight lot over. The window reads the campaign day at that moment and nothing has counted down: a lot past its due day has 1D+4 × 10% taken off the fare (Core p.241), and the card says what was docked. The Credit transfer opens with the sum due, and the lot leaves the hold when you confirm it.

Ashore puts a booking off the ship. No money moves, since the fare was paid at booking. A low-berth booking's card carries a Revival check button. Select the token making the check and target the passenger, whose END DM it borrows, and it opens the Routine (6+) check of Core p.158 with the ship's own modifiers. The DM for a non-human passenger is stated on the card and not applied, because no document says who is one.

@UUID[Compendium.mgt2.demo-items.Item.demoCargoLot0001]{Demo — Cargo Lot} and @UUID[Compendium.mgt2.demo-items.Item.demoPassageOutbd]{Demo — Outbound Passage} show both Items. Do not write baggage, fare or the low-berth flag on a passage by hand: the class derives them.

The window reports passengers and never writes them onto the ship's four typed counts, which are ignored once a booking exists.

Speculative trade

Open it from the token controls, or from a world's sheet with Trade here, which seeds the world for you. The window takes one market and one ship. The rule of the page is that the world's codes drive everything, so check the Trade codes here line first. If the profile is miscopied, everything after it is too.

The stop runs in the order of the buttons along the foot.

Find a supplier is the check of Core p.241, made by a Traveller and not by the window. The Searching Traveller list offers the ship's stations, then whoever is selected, then your own character. It opens the ordinary prompt with the Starport DM and the month's searches on it as waivable modifiers, and rolls how long the hunt took. It uses Broker, or Streetwise for a black market, or Admin for an online supplier on a TL8+ world, and the two boxes on the form choose. A failed search stops nothing: the screen does not gate the shelf on it.

Roll the shelf rolls the tonnage of every line and the extra random goods, one per point of Population (Core p.242-243). Below the shelf, Also in stock lists the random rows. Black market supplier adds the illegal goods that match, and draws the random rows from the illegal ones.

Roll both prices rolls 3D for the purchase and 3D for the sale at once, since a crew sells and buys at one counter. Pick a line on the shelf and the two columns below it show every term of the reading. Only the largest DM of each column counts, and the column that makes a cargo cheap here is subtracted when it is sold (Core p.243).

Four controls change the reading. Broker skill and Their Broker are the two sides of the negotiation, the second starting at the book's assumed 2. Banned at law is the Law Level the goods are banned at, for a smuggled cargo: the difference from this world's Law Level replaces the Sale DM where it is higher (Core p.243). Blank means nobody bans them, and that is a different statement from Law Level 0. Hired local broker adds their DM+2 to the negotiation, and takes 10% of the gross, or 20% for illegal goods (Core p.242).

Buy the lot needs a GM, a ship and both rolls. It opens the Credit transfer to debit the crew, and the cargo lot lands in the hold when you confirm, remembering the price it was bought at. A broker's cut rides on top of a purchase. A good bought is gone from this supplier until you re-roll the shelf.

In the hold lists what the ship carries, each lot priced off its own stored Sale DMs against this market once the prices are rolled. Sell credits the crew and removes the lot, and a broker's cut comes out of what it fetches. Freight lots are listed and never offered, since they are carried for a fare and are not the crew's to sell.

Walk away refuses the price. On a dropped world it shuts that supplier for a month (Core p.243), and the world's sheet shows the day it reopens.

Exotics are outside these rules: no price, no tonnage, no DM. Post to chat puts the reading on the log.

What a dropped world remembers

Two facts of a stop outlive the window, and only with a world in the slot and write access to it: the searches made there this month, and a refused supplier. The searches cost DM−1 each on the next (Core p.241), and while a world is in the slot it owns that count, so the box beside it goes dead. Each search stamps the world. With no world, type the count yourself and nothing is stored. Both facts are read against the campaign day, with a month of 28 days. Searches count within the same calendar month and a refusal runs 28 days from the day it was made, so advancing the day is what lets them lapse.

Players can open this window, read it and make the search. A world hands them read access only, so their search is not stamped unless the referee has given them more. The world sheet carries controls for both facts, for a referee working from there.

The Credit transfer

Every sum that moves here goes through one window, which is also open to you from a macro as game.mgt2.creditSplit. It is the referee's; a Traveller's own sheet opens a gift version of it for their purse.

Opened from a trade, it arrives filled in: the sum, the direction, the reason, and the ship's crew as the roster. Only character Actors have purses, so a crew member who is an NPC drops out of the list.

  • Debit takes the money out, and what a Traveller cannot pay becomes debt on their sheet. Credit pays it in, and repays no debt.
  • Add payers with + Selected, + Party or + Crew, or by dropping a Traveller on the list; a dropped ship adds its crew.
  • Even splits equally. Dragging one share moves the others, and the lock fixes a share so no other row's move can change it.
  • Cover the shortfall moves what short payers cannot meet onto unlocked payers who have the cash.
  • Rounding is in whole credits and the window names who took the odd one.

The button stays dead until the whole sum is assigned. Applying posts a card with every share. Show balances and Private decide who sees what on that card, and two world settings choose where each starts.

What this leaves to you

  • Whether the crew may trade at all this week. Nothing times a search, a sale or a booking, and every stated duration is a line on a card.
  • Cargo loss. A Cargo critical is stated on the ship and takes nothing out of the hold.
  • Getting caught. The consequences of smuggling are yours (Core p.243).
  • The ship's own bills, which are on its @UUID[Compendium.mgt2.guide.JournalEntry.3wd9e5Iz4A9besSS.JournalEntryPage.IQl36fl0PKjut4bg]{Finance tab}. Revenue goes to the crew's purses; a ship has no cash balance.

The voyage screen flies one ship one leg at a time. It keeps a stop, the next stop and a list of names after that; it rolls the two checks of a jump, debits the tank and reads a misjump. It does not keep time. Nothing here advances the campaign day, schedules an arrival or bills a month. The clock is yours, and the Arrive button is how you say it has moved.

Open it from the menu in a spacecraft sheet's title bar, or by right-clicking the ship in the Actors directory. There is one screen per ship. An owner of the ship can change it; anyone else who can see it reads it.

The leg

The strip across the top is the route. Here and Next are the two ends of the one leg that exists, with the parsecs between them.

Drop a world Actor on either end to link it. Its name, profile, trade codes and travel zone then read from the document, and clicking the name opens it. A world is not required: with no document, type a name in the box, and that name is the stop. @UUID[Compendium.mgt2.demo-actors.Actor.demoWorldBellwth]{Demo — Bellweather} is a world to practise with. Next can be cleared with its cross; a ship with nothing planned is still somewhere.

Parsecs is typed, and it belongs to the pair. Where both ends are worlds placed on the map by sector and hex, the distance they imply appears beside the box as a reading, and it does not overwrite what you typed. The floor is 1, since a shorter jump counts as jump-1 for the DM and for the fuel alike (Core p.157). Linking a new Next puts the figure back to 1.

Then is the queue. Drop a world on it to file the name. Click a queued stop to make it Next, and its cross forgets it. A queued stop keeps a name and the world dropped, and nothing else. It carries no distance, because a distance belongs to a pair and nobody has chosen the pair yet.

The line under the strip reads the leg: fuel this jump, the Astrogation DM, the time in jump, the Jump Control rating the distance calls for, the drive's range and the travel zone at the far end. A leg longer than the drive's rating goes red with a note. It is a warning only, and the checks can still be rolled.

Advancing

Arrive at… is the only thing that moves the leg. Next becomes Here, the head of the queue becomes Next, and the parsecs go back to 1 for a pair nobody has measured. It writes nothing else: no fuel, no day and no passengers ashore. A failed jump does not move it, and a clean one does not either. Press it when your story says they have arrived. If a misjump put them somewhere else, set Here yourself.

Fuel

The panel shows two different quantities. The cap is the tank's design size, set on the ship's Design tab. The level is what is really aboard. The first never moves, and the second starts at zero on a new ship, which is why a fresh hull's Jump button is dead.

The In the tank box is the only way to add fuel. There is no refuelling action: skimming and buying are yours to run, and typing a level costs nobody anything. The ship block quotes the price per ton and of a full tank, for the grade the ship's refined tick states (Core p.154). The fuel grade each end's starport offers is printed in the Both ends block, off the world's own profile.

Where Here's starport sells both grades, which a Class C port does under the classCRefinedFuel optional rule (Companion p.133), a Grade taken on strip sits under the box: refined at Cr500 a ton or unrefined at Cr100. It sets the ship's refined tick, so the price quoted and the jump's DM−2 for unrefined fuel follow it.

Under the box the screen says what this jump burns and what it leaves. The burn is 10% of hull per parsec of this leg (Core p.157), not per parsec of the drive's rating. The ship sheet's jumps in tank is the other reading: full-range jumps at the design figure.

The jump

A jump is a chain of two checks (Core p.157). Each has its button in the rail, and a second one on the roster row of its station.

Plot is an Easy (4+) Astrogation check, at DM−1 per parsec, made by whoever is linked at the station whose role is the astrogator. Jump is an Easy (4+) Engineer (j-drive) check by the engineer. Both open @UUID[Compendium.mgt2.guide.JournalEntry.3wd9e5Iz4A9besSS.JournalEntryPage.AFpVHfj7ijV7S9ct]{the ordinary roll prompt}, with the parsec DM or the unrefined-fuel DM on it as a modifier you can untick. To carry the first Effect into the second, choose the Plot card on the prompt's chain row; the chain is not armed for you.

Both refuse with a message when no linked sheet is at that station. A name-only row will not do, since there is no skill level to read. The station is found by the role's Crew position field, so see @UUID[Compendium.mgt2.guide.JournalEntry.3wd9e5Iz4A9besSS.JournalEntryPage.IQl36fl0PKjut4bg]{Spacecraft} if the screen cannot find your engineer. Drop a Traveller on a roster row here to seat them; that writes the ship's roster.

The fuel leaves with the Jump roll. Posting the Engineer check debits the burn, whatever the check scored. Dismissing the prompt debits nothing, and the button refuses outright if the tank cannot cover the burn. No other roll touches the fuel.

Two chips beside the Jump button are reminders only: the DM per month behind on maintenance, and the 100-diameter limit. The book prints both (Core p.157). The sheet keeps the ship's service date, but neither reaches the roll, so add them on the prompt.

A critical reaches the jump by itself (Core p.170). A J-Drive at Severity 1 puts a chip beside Jump and its DM−2 on the check, as a modifier you can untick; Plot uses no drive and takes neither. A drive that is disabled or destroyed greys Jump and the screen says why. The same DM and the same refusal meet an Engineer (j-drive) action pressed on the roster or the space combat screen (Core p.171). Lower the severity on the sheet once the drive is mended.

Two rulesets

The two procedures for reading a jump differ in shape. Each ship declares its own on this screen, and a new ship takes the world's Jump procedure for new ships rule.

Stored valueMeaning
coreCore
companionCompanion

Core reads the Effect of the Engineer check alone (Core p.157-158). The two rolls are a chain, as above.

Companion reads both Effects, and it reads them on every jump, not only a failed one (Companion p.150-153). A misjump there is the sum of the two, so nothing chains and neither roll resolves first. Leave the chain row alone under this ruleset.

Changing the ruleset discards a reading already made.

Reading a jump

The misjump block at the bottom of the panel is a readout: nothing it finds is written to the ship. Rolling the checks fills in its Effects, or you can type them for a jump flown on paper. Press Read the jump, then Post to put the result on the chat log with its dice.

Under Core, a clean check says so and the table's outcome is stated otherwise, with any dice it asks for already rolled. Two optional rules touch it: Perceived time on a late jump adds the extra time the crew experiences, and The merciful referee's outcome adds a note on the worst band (Core p.158).

Under Companion, the block rolls both variance tables, tests for a misjump, and then rolls whichever consequence tables the pair has earned. It prints the verdict, each table's read, what the page printed and the result, so you can check it against your book. It has one more input: gravity at entry, which the screen cannot know.

What the block reports stays in the block. An emergence point, a late arrival, a wrecked drive or a percentage of Hull lost per day all wait for you, on the leg, the ship's Criticals block or your calendar.

What this screen leaves to you

  • The date. The campaign day is a world setting, and you move it.
  • Refuelling, and paying for it.

A Region is Foundry's tool for "while you are here, this happens to you". The system adds four behaviours for the environment. Draw a Region on a scene, add a behaviour to it, and fill in its fields.

TypeSub-types
GravityNone
RadiationNone
TemperatureNone
VacuumNone

Why nothing ticks

This is the surprise, so it comes first. The system has no clock. It never decides that an hour has passed, and Foundry gives a Region no event that says so. A Region hears about a token crossing its edge, and about a combat round starting. That is all it can react to.

So a hazard does one of three things.

WhenWhat happensBehaviours
A token entersIt runs once, at the crossingGravity, Radiation
A combat round startsIt runs for each combatant's token insideVacuum, Temperature at Per round
Anything slowerNothing. The interval is stated and you apply itTemperature at any other interval

A Traveller crossing hard vacuum without a suit outside combat takes nothing automatically, and neither does a token inside the Region that is not a combatant. If the table is not in rounds, you roll the damage yourself. A wrong number the system applied on its own would be worse than none, because nobody would check it.

An entry runs on the client of whoever moved the token, and a round start on the referee's, so a round hazard needs a referee connected. Damage from a Region comes straight off the damage chain, with no armour step, and posts an Environment card.

Who a hazard reaches

Temperature and Vacuum wound a person: a Traveller or an NPC. The book's rule names a Traveller, and a hull is what a Traveller stands inside (Core p.82), so a vehicle or a spacecraft takes nothing and gets no card. A robot is not wounded as a person either: see Vacuum for the rule Robot Handbook p.34 gives it.

Radiation reaches a Traveller, an NPC and a robot, because each keeps a count of rads. An NPC reads the Traveller's table, and a creature takes the immediate column on its Hits with no END to lose. A robot takes the dose on its brain and follows the same radiation optional rule (see @UUID[Compendium.mgt2.guide.JournalEntry.3wd9e5Iz4A9besSS.JournalEntryPage.5anXbSCX3G4DE4Nm]{Robots}). Gravity reaches any actor that makes checks.

Several hazards at once

A token can stand in two Regions, and one Region can carry two behaviours. Foundry runs them all at the same moment. The system takes them one at a time for each actor, so each lands on the wound the last one left and none is lost. Each posts its own card.

Gravity

The gravity behaviour names a band.

Stored valueMeaning
microMicro-gravity
minimalMinimal gravity
veryLowVery low gravity
lowLow gravity
standardStandard gravity
highHigh gravity
extremeExtreme gravity

On entry the token's actor gains an Active Effect named for the band: a DM on every check on a high-gravity world, or on physical checks only on a low-gravity one (Core p.80-81, Companion p.59-64). Standard gravity does nothing. An actor gets one effect per Region, however often it crosses.

Leaving the Region does not end it. The penalty lasts until the Traveller acclimatises, which the effect's description states (Core p.80), and that is a matter of weeks. You end it by deleting the effect from the actor's Effects tab. On the prompt a low-gravity effect appears as its own row, and follows the characteristic chosen. The microgravity band also brings the attack line on @UUID[Compendium.mgt2.guide.JournalEntry.3wd9e5Iz4A9besSS.JournalEntryPage.AFpVHfj7ijV7S9ct]{the roll prompt}.

Temperature

Temperature states the degrees, the damage and how often.

Stored valueMeaning
roundPer round
minutePer minute
hourPer hour
dayPer day

Only Per round is applied on its own, at each round's start. Every other interval is a statement on the behaviour for you to read and apply (Companion p.83-84). A new Temperature behaviour starts at Per hour with no damage, so it does nothing until you set it.

Negated by lists gear by name. A token whose actor has an item of exactly that name equipped is left alone. Carrying it in a pack does not count (Core p.82). The name has to match the Item's; capitals do not matter.

Vacuum

Two books print two systems, and the How vacuum exposure is worked out optional rule chooses between them (Core p.82, Companion p.65-71). Both run at each round's start.

Stored valueMeaning
hardHard vacuum
partialPartial vacuum
minimalThin atmosphere
  • Under the Core reading, the Damage field applies each round. Hard vacuum escalates: if the field reads 1D, the second round is 2D and the third 3D. Sealed suit is not read at all, so a Traveller in a vacc suit standing in this Region is hurt too. Under this reading, keep suited tokens out of the Region or out of the combat.
  • Under the Companion reading, a table decides, and the Damage field is not read. The row is the state of the equipped suit named under Sealed suit: intact is complete protection, a breach is set on the suit's own sheet, and no suit at all is the No Protection row. Where the table's entry is an interval longer than a round, the card states it once, on the first round, and you apply it.

Each token counts its own exposure, and leaving the Region resets that count. The wound stays. A round number means nothing outside its combat, so a count left over from an earlier fight starts again too. A round you skip over is not charged, and the next round hits at the severity its number says.

A robot follows Robot Handbook p.34. It is not wounded. On entry, in or out of combat, its endurance halves for as long as it stays, and a card states the malfunction check it owes every hour, or every two with hostile, corrosive or insidious environment protection, at DM-2 past 100 °C either way. You roll that check: 8+ on 2D, a failure being a Severity 1 critical (Robot Handbook p.108). Vacuum Environment Protection stops all of it. An android counts as a robot. A robot with Biological ticked takes what a Traveller takes, on its Hits, unless it carries that protection, and it takes no Temperature hazard from a Region: the book's sentence speaks of vacuum alone.

Only the printed English names of those options read. Vacuum sealing, beside Biological in the robot's header, answers instead: a row written in another language, or a design with the protection as standard and no row, such as a nanorobot (Robot Handbook p.83). Left blank, it reads Rows: and what the rows gave, so a row that went unread shows there.

Radiation

Radiation is a dose on entry, the one hazard that suits Foundry's model unchanged (Core p.81-82).

Dose is a number or dice, written as the books print it, such as 2D×20. Absorbed by the region comes off first, for a Region behind shielding. The Traveller's own Rad score comes off next, and the card reports what reached them, with any immediate and permanent effect. A dose the Region can not read warns you and leaves the token moving.

Every entry is a new dose, so a token that walks out and back takes another. Longer exposure at a reactor or under a flare is yours to apply, from the sheet's exposure control.

With the radiation optional rule off, the Region is silent. Nothing is rolled, no dose is recorded and no card is posted, for a robot as for a Traveller. A Radiation weapon's dose stops at the same switch.

  • Reactor wash is Radiation: Dose 3D6×10, Absorbed by the region 30. Walk her in. The move waits for the roll, and the card reports what reached her. Walking out heals nothing, and walking back in is a second dose.

An Active Effect is a change to an actor's numbers that something else is responsible for: a charm, a gravity band, a dose. This system uses Foundry's own mechanism with three additions: a configuration window that exposes the phase, @item, and drugs.

The whole page comes down to one question, so here it is first. If your effect seems to do nothing, look at its phase.

Where an effect lives

On an Item, an effect is what the Item does. It transfers to whoever holds the Item. Gear with an Equipped toggle, which is armour, weapons and equipment, augments included, transfers only while it is equipped: padding in a backpack changes nothing. An Item dropped on a sheet arrives unequipped, so press its shield. Add an effect on the item's Effects tab in edit mode. Worked example: @UUID[Compendium.mgt2.demo-items.Item.demoTrinketFob01]{Demo — Lucky Fob}.

On an Actor, an effect is a condition it has acquired. The Actor's Effects tab lists these together with everything its Items transfer, naming the source of each. Add one there at any time.

A row shows the effect's changes, each with its phase, and its duration.

  • Enable or disable is the effect's own switch.
  • Suspend or resume is the referee's pause, kept apart so that an effect a player turned off and one the table is ignoring for a scene stay different things. Both leave the effect inert.
  • Edit and Delete do as they say. The rows behind status icons offer no delete, for the reason given at the foot of this page.

The configuration window

The Changes tab has one row per change.

ColumnMeans
KeyThe field written, such as system.modifiers.check.custom
TypeHow it is written, such as add or override
ValueA number, or a reference such as @item.protection
PhaseWhen it is written
PriorityThe order within a phase

Foundry hides the Phase as a fixed input. This window makes it a select, because it decides whether the change survives.

The phase

An actor is prepared in order, each time anything changes:

  1. Stored data loads.
  2. Initial changes are written.
  3. The system computes everything derived.
  4. Final changes are written.

Step 3 overwrites whatever a derived field held. A change aimed at a derived field in the initial phase is wiped the moment it lands. It raises no error and no warning, and it looks like a broken effect. Worked example, two effects side by side: @UUID[Compendium.mgt2.demo-items.Item.demoStandingDM01]{Demo — Standing DM}.

Aim atPhaseWhat follows
system.characteristics.<key>.effectInitialMaximum, current value, DM and life all follow. Not for powered armour's STR and DEX: Core p.102 keeps that bonus off the damage track, so type it on the armour itself, and delete any dm change a suit was given before
system.modifiers.check.customInitialA DM on every check
system.modifiers.initiative.customInitialA DM on Initiative only
system.modifiers.skills.<slug>.effectInitialA DM on one skill and its specialities, such as pilot or gun-combat: a row on the prompt, ticked while that skill is chosen. On an actor without the skill, a request naming it ticks the row on the untrained answer, and a free roll shows it unticked for the roller to tick. It follows the actor who rolls: at a ship's station, at a vehicle's wheel and on a supplier search, as on the sheet. A fleet's rolls have no actor behind them, so nothing reaches those
system.characteristics.<key>.valueFinalThe number shown moves, and nothing else does

The first row is the one to reach for. effect exists to be written by effects, and everything derived reads it. A final write to value comes after the DM was computed, so the sheet shows a higher score with the old DM. Use the final phase only where you want the printed figure changed and nothing computed from it.

A DM aimed at modifiers.check appears on @UUID[Compendium.mgt2.guide.JournalEntry.3wd9e5Iz4A9besSS.JournalEntryPage.AFpVHfj7ijV7S9ct]{the roll prompt} as the Actor modifier row, where it can be waived, and it reaches every check. A DM that belongs to one skill goes on that skill's key in the table above, on an augment's Skill field, or in the prompt's custom DM.

@item

An effect normally reads the actor's data, so the number a trait scales on, such as the armour's protection or the talent's level, is out of its reach. Here an effect transferred from an Item can write @item in its value to read that Item:

@item.protection
@item.level

The reference reaches the Item's system data, so a bonus follows the Item it comes from when its figure changes. It works only on an effect that lives on an Item. On an Actor's own effect there is no Item to read, and Foundry drops the whole change with a console warning and nothing shown on the sheet.

Why a drug does nothing on the shelf

Worked example: @UUID[Compendium.mgt2.demo-items.Item.demoDrugSteady01]{Demo — Steadying Dose}.

Other Items' effects work while they are carried, or while equipped where the Item has that toggle. A drug's never do. They are a template, and the trigger is taking it, not owning the box. So the row on the drug's own sheet reads as inactive however you set it, which is correct.

Take a dose, on the drug's sheet, does this:

  1. Rolls the Onset and Duration, if they read as a time, such as 10 minutes or 1D hours.
  2. Copies the drug's effects onto the Traveller, carrying that duration. A drug with no effects leaves a plain row named for it, so that the dose can be seen and ended.
  3. Spends one of the quantity. With none left, the button is refused.
  4. Adds one to the Traveller's count of doses of that drug, which outlasts the last dose being swallowed.
  5. Posts a dose card.

The copies belong to the Traveller and work like any effect, with one exception.

An onset that reads as a time means the copy starts disabled. Its row says starts in the printed interval. Nothing starts it for you: when the time has passed in your game, press the row's enable control.

Nothing ends a dose for you either. The system runs no clock, so a duration is shown and you judge it. The row of a dose carries an End this dose control. It removes the effect, and runs whatever the drug leaves behind: a condition is stated on a card, and damage is rolled and taken straight off the damage chain. Plain deletion removes the effect and skips that step.

Statuses

The token status icons are Active Effects too. Three of the sheet's states are mirrored by an icon: encumbered, unconscious and dead. Those are derived from wounds and load. A hand-placed icon for one of them is taken back at once, because the icon is a readout. Fatigue is stored, and works in both directions: the sheet's tick sets the icon, and the token HUD sets the tick. These mirrored rows appear on the Effects tab with no delete control.

Other icons, such as prone and stunned, are Foundry's own and move no number.

The other way effects arrive is a gravity Region, which places one on entry; see @UUID[Compendium.mgt2.guide.JournalEntry.3wd9e5Iz4A9besSS.JournalEntryPage.NXswhOUqMQZKe9lQ]{Regions and hazards}.

The quickest way to learn what a correctly filled document looks like is to open one. Between them the three demo packs hold a filled example of every Actor type, of nearly every Item type, with the common variants of each, and a Scene with its Regions. All of it is invented: the demo world, its careers and its ships come from no book, so nothing here can be mistaken for printed text.

Each demo document stands on one cliff, a point where a referee building their own content tends to fall. The tour below is assembled from the notes those documents carry. The notes do not show on the sheets, so this page is where you read them.

How to read an entry

  • The heading links to the document. A sheet opened beside your own work is the way to use it.
  • The bold line is the cliff.
  • The list says what the document teaches, field by field. A field is written as the data stores it, such as frame.steps or flags.mgt2.chargen, which is also how a macro or a module would reach it.
  • The quotation is the trap: the thing that fails silently, or the field that looks required and is not.

To change a demo document, import it into your world and edit the copy. The packs belong to the system, so your edits have no place in them. Rename the copy once it stops being an example.

A demo document still in its pack answers only to its name. The lists that creation builds by searching, such as the careers always open, the skills an open pick offers and the voucher window, skip the demo packs. Import a document into the world to put it on those lists.

The tour

@UUID[Compendium.mgt2.demo-actors.Actor.demoCharTravellr]{Demo — Traveller}

skills are Items, and a species feeds .auto

  • A skill is a talent Item with subType: skill embedded on the Actor. There is no system.skills anywhere in this system, and everything that reads a skill matches it by name, but for roll.skill, which holds the id of one.
  • personal.species holds the id of the species Item embedded below it — the Actor stores a pointer and copies nothing.
  • A career on a Traveller is the same Item type as the career in the compendium; the record half at the bottom of it is what says which one this is.
  • The inventory is embedded Items pointing at each other: a round names its weapon, a stack names its bag, an augment names a skill, an armour names the skill it needs.

Not one characteristic writes .auto. The species feeds that field, and a value written beside it is ADDED rather than replaced — so it grows every time the derivation runs. base, damage and show are the three a document may write; auto, effect, max and value all derive. The Sidearm's roll.skill is the id of Gun Combat (slug) on this Actor, a local graph: dropped on another it opens on Not proficient until it is bound again.

@UUID[Compendium.mgt2.demo-actors.Actor.demoNpcDockOffcr]{Demo — Dock Officer}

_preCreate never runs for a packed document

Everything under config, and every characteristics.*.show below, is written by hand because _preCreate does not run for a document that arrives from a pack. a creature is one Actor type with a different configuration

  • behaviour.diet and behaviour.pattern are the two fields that say how it hunts and what it wants.
  • group.count is a pack of them on one sheet: value is how many are left, max how many there were.

A creature needs characteristics.hits.base above 0 AND the string hits in config.damageOrder. three graphs of ids, and none of them stores a name

Foundry shows one compendium at a time. The explorer is one search across every compendium you can see: the world's, the system's and every module's. It answers where a thing is and copies nothing. A library spread over a dozen packs is the case it exists for.

Open it with the Explore button at the top of the Compendium tab. Anyone can use it, and each user sees only the packs visible to them. It covers compendiums only: documents in the world's own sidebar do not appear.

Search and filters

The search box matches any part of a name. The other filters narrow what is left.

  • Document picks a class, such as Actor or Item.
  • Type and Sub-type list what the shown packs hold. Each option carries the count of rows it would leave, so a choice that leads nowhere can be seen before it is made.
  • Scale appears only when weapons are among the rows, since nothing else has one.
  • Tech Level takes a minimum, a maximum or both. A blank box is no bound, not zero. A row with no numeric Tech Level drops out as soon as either bound is set.

Reset clears the filters and shows every pack again. Nothing here is saved: what you are looking for is a question, not a preference.

The pack list

The pack list is two things at once: the filter for where to search, and the progress of the indexes. Packs are grouped as this world, the system and modules, with all and none for each group. Each row gives its document class and size, and a padlock marks a pack that is read-only.

The results

Rows sort by name, type, Tech Level or compendium. Click a column to sort, and again to reverse it. A Tech Level sorts as a number, and rows without one go last.

The list draws the first 200 matches and says so when there are more. Narrow the search to reach the rest.

Drag a row onto a sheet and it behaves as a drag from the compendium itself. A padlock is no obstacle: it stops writing into a pack, not taking a copy out of one. Click a name to open the document's sheet with no import.

What the index costs

A compendium's index is what Foundry can read about a document without loading it. Names are there from the moment the world loads, so the search box answers at once.

The system adds five fields to the index of every Actor and Item pack: Tech Level, sub-type, weapon scale, cost, and whether a weapon is melee. Those arrive only when a pack's index is fetched, which costs one request per pack the first time the explorer opens. Two things follow.

  • The window says what it does not know yet. It counts the indexes still arriving. A Tech Level on its way prints as an ellipsis, where a dash means the row has none.
  • A row is withheld rather than guessed. While a sub-type, scale or Tech Level filter is set, rows from a pack still arriving stay out of the list and are counted as withheld. They join as their pack lands.

A pack whose index fails stays out of those readings and the rest keep working. The error goes to the console.

The same five fields feed the voucher window at mustering out, which is how a Benefit's credit and TL ceilings can filter a whole library. See @UUID[Compendium.mgt2.guide.JournalEntry.3wd9e5Iz4A9besSS.JournalEntryPage.XAy8tHQw02RmRtPC]{Character creation}.

A macro can open the window with its filters already set. See @UUID[Compendium.mgt2.guide.JournalEntry.3wd9e5Iz4A9besSS.JournalEntryPage.U0ZcNzi5dw5MPnBN]{Macros and the API}.

The books print options, variants and whole alternative procedures, and a table plays some of them and not others. Every one the system implements is a world setting in a single window, and the sheets and dialogs show what you adopted and nothing else.

Open it from the system's settings with the Optional and variant rules entry. Only the referee can.

The window

Each page of the window covers one domain, and the rail counts the rules on it. A second figure on the rail counts how many you have moved off their default, and those rows are marked.

  • The search box lists every matching rule across all pages.
  • Changed only does the same for rules off their default, which is the quick answer to what is different at this table?
  • The information button on a row unfolds its explanation.

A rule comes in one of four shapes: a switch, a set of boxes, a choice, or a number. Each change is written as you make it, with no save button, and the window stays open. Open sheets and dialogs redraw at once, on every client.

What a change does

  • Nothing is deleted. Turning a rule off hides what it drew. What is already on a sheet stays there and comes back when you switch the rule on again.
  • Rolls already posted are left alone. A chat card records the rules in force when it was rolled.
  • Not everything starts off. A default is the reading the books best support, so a rule the books print as a rule starts on. Check the table below before assuming a feature is missing or switched on.
  • An upgraded world keeps what it had. Where a world from an earlier version first meets a rule that hides something it was already showing, that rule is set to preserve the old behaviour. A new world takes the default.

Interpretations

The last page of the window is different. An interpretation is not an option a book prints. It marks a place where the book is silent or ambiguous and the software had to take a reading. Each one holds the most common reading already, so change it only where your table rules otherwise.

The optional map High Guard prints beside the fleet battle rules: eight rings of range around a fixed point, each cut into quadrants and sectors. Placing a fleet on it writes the range between fleets that the battle screen already reads, so switching it off leaves every range where it stands and returns the map to being typed by hand.		OffHigh Guard p.122-124

Offers an automation part; the row it carries moves the crew requirement by its printed percentage, and a role that needs one body still needs one.		OffTraveller Companion p.178

A salvo says which of the four the referee put in the air. A dogfight missile cannot be fired past Close and attacks at DM+4 inside it; an interceptor cannot be fired past Short and attacks at DM+2. Worth knowing

The palette. All five palette settings are per client, so one player's choice repaints only their own screen. The ground decides light or dark for this system's windows, and by default it follows Foundry's own colour scheme.

The campaign day. This is the only calendar the system has, and nothing advances it but you. Speculative trade, freight deadlines and ship maintenance all read it, so a campaign that never touches it will see those stand still. See @UUID[Compendium.mgt2.guide.JournalEntry.3wd9e5Iz4A9besSS.JournalEntryPage.ZPr9rPt1v4Xq0HqD]{What this system deliberately does not do}.

The skills package. The pool for creation's shared skills package is a world setting with no entry here. It is typed on the closing screen, where it is used.

The system exposes its rolls and windows on game.mgt2, so a macro or a module can do what a button does. No macro pack ships. This page shows what there is to call.

Whatever a macro calls runs as the user who pressed it, with that user's permissions. A call that opens a dialog opens it on that user's screen.

Dragging to the hotbar

Drag a skill, a weapon, an armour, a computer or a disease from a sheet onto the hotbar and the slot rolls it. The Item must be on an Actor: an Item in the sidebar or a compendium gets Foundry's own behaviour.

Each drop makes a script macro whose whole body is one call, and that is the simplest call in the API:

game.mgt2.rollItem("Actor.AbCdEf.Item.GhIjKl");

The macro opens the same roll prompt the sheet opens. A skill goes to the prompt's skill row, and a psionic talent brings its reach and PSI strips with it. The same Item dropped on a second slot reuses its macro rather than cloning it. A locked hotbar takes no drop. A macro names the Item by its id, so one made on a Traveller does not follow a copy of that Traveller.

Rolling

game.mgt2.roll(actor, what, token) is the door every check on a sheet goes through. It opens @UUID[Compendium.mgt2.guide.JournalEntry.3wd9e5Iz4A9besSS.JournalEntryPage.AFpVHfj7ijV7S9ct]{the roll prompt} and posts the card, and what says what is being rolled:

whatRolls
{ roll: "characteristic", characteristic: "endurance" }a characteristic check
{ roll: "skill", skill: item.id }a skill, by the id of its Item on that Actor
{ roll: "initiative" }initiative
{ roll: "psionic", itemId: item.id }a psionic talent
{ itemId: item.id }a weapon, an armour, a computer or a disease

Two more keys go with any of these. difficulty sets the rung the prompt opens on, and modifiers adds rows of your own, each { key, label, dm }, which the player can untick. The optional third argument is the token the roll comes from.

const actor = canvas.tokens.controlled[0]?.actor ?? game.user.character;
if ( actor ) game.mgt2.roll(actor, {
    roll: "characteristic",
    characteristic: "endurance",
    difficulty: "Difficult",
    modifiers: [{ key: "storm", label: "Storm", dm: -1 }]
});

A check with no prompt

game.mgt2.Checks rolls and scores with nobody asked. resolve takes a formula and a difficulty key, or a bare target number, and gives back the roll and its Effect. post puts the card in chat. Passing secret: true whispers it to the referee.

const actor = game.user.character;
const outcome = await game.mgt2.Checks.resolve({ formula: "2d6+1", difficulty: "Average" });
await game.mgt2.Checks.post(outcome, { actor, label: "Recon", rollObjectName: "Recon", secret: true });

outcome.effect is the Effect, outcome.band its band and outcome.roll the Foundry Roll. Checks.modifiers reduces a list of [name, dm] rows to the terms a formula reads.

World profiles

parseUwp reads the bare nine characters of a profile into an object and returns null for anything else, so a full catalogue row or a trailing zone letter does not parse. formatUwp turns the object back into the printed line.

const uwp = game.mgt2.parseUwp("A788899-C");
uwp.techLevel;                 // 12
game.mgt2.formatUwp(uwp);      // "A788899-C"

Roll requests

game.mgt2.request has three members. parse reads the words of an @Request[…] link into a demand, post creates a request card from a full payload, and answer answers one line of a posted card. For most macros parse and @UUID[Compendium.mgt2.guide.JournalEntry.3wd9e5Iz4A9besSS.JournalEntryPage.TUwYdm40vTQJiuSJ]{the Docket} are enough, since the Docket resolves the skill against its roster before anything is sent:

game.mgt2.docket(game.mgt2.request.parse('Recon dc=routine why="Spot the tail"'));

Fleet battles

fleetAttack is the attack path of @UUID[Compendium.mgt2.guide.JournalEntry.3wd9e5Iz4A9besSS.JournalEntryPage.qyA5mTeKnbGAu6s6]{fleet battles}: resolveStandard, resolveSpinal, resolveMissiles, resolveIon, apply and criticals, plus the readings bandBetween, inRange, armourAgainst, factor and damage. The attacks, apply and criticals refuse while the Fleet battles rule is off. criticals with roll: false writes nothing and only reads, so it still answers. fleetWeaponRow, fleetWeaponRows and fleetBatteries read a spacecraft's weapons as the Fleet Ship Sheet prints them.

Reading the table's configuration

An optional rule is a world setting under the key rule.<name>. A switch reads as a boolean, a set of boxes as a Set, a choice as its key and a cap as a number. To list every rule key from the console:

[...game.settings.settings.keys()].filter(key => key.startsWith("mgt2.rule."));
game.settings.get("mgt2", "rule.psionics");

The campaign day is game.settings.get("mgt2", "campaignDay"), and a macro may set it: nothing else will.

CONFIG.MGT2 holds every registry the system runs on, such as characteristics, difficulties and the crew roles. A registry is frozen, so read it and do not write to it. game.mgt2.TravellerActor and game.mgt2.TravellerItem are the document classes.

The system fires no hooks of its own. A module that wants to react to a roll or a term listens to Foundry's document hooks, such as createChatMessage or updateActor.

pages.name: What this system deliberately does not do

text.content:
Every item on this page was considered and turned down. If you came here looking for a button, this is the place to find out that it is not hidden, it was left out, and why.

One idea runs through most of them: the system works out what a rule is worth, and you decide when it applies.

Nothing runs on a clock

The system never schedules anything. It does not read Foundry's world time and has no tick and no advance time control. Where a rule runs on an interval, the interval is printed and the referee applies it. A disease shows how often it is rolled, a drug shows how long it lasts, and a hazard shows its interval.

A clock would be one more thing to manage, and it would be wrong the first time a party crossed three weeks in a sentence.

Combat rounds are the one exception, because you are already advancing them by hand. A hazard Region applies itself only on its per round rows (see @UUID[Compendium.mgt2.guide.JournalEntry.3wd9e5Iz4A9besSS.JournalEntryPage.NXswhOUqMQZKe9lQ]{Regions and hazards}). On any longer interval it states the rule and leaves it with you, which is why a region of cold can sit on a scene doing nothing while the party walks through it for an hour.

The campaign day is the one number that stands in for a calendar. It is a world setting you type, and nothing moves it: not a jump, not a voyage, not a rest. @UUID[Compendium.mgt2.guide.JournalEntry.3wd9e5Iz4A9besSS.JournalEntryPage.HZ0VLzZ4geAh88qk]{Speculative trade} reads it for a supplier's month, freight for a delivery date, and a ship for the maintenance it owes. See @UUID[Compendium.mgt2.guide.JournalEntry.3wd9e5Iz4A9besSS.JournalEntryPage.L1PCQIr60xQbIsD1]{Settings}.

Nothing bills you

A ship's sheet works out its mortgage, its maintenance and its running costs. Nothing collects them. There is no end-of-period button, because deciding that a period has ended is the referee's call and a ship's accounts are rarely that tidy.

A ship has no cash balance. Money belongs to people, and it outlives any one voyage and any one ship. How a crew shares costs is an agreement at the table and not a field. The transfer screen moves credits between the purses you name, on demand, and that is the only thing in the system that does so.

Skipped maintenance stays on paper. The ship counts the periods overdue since its last recorded service, against the campaign day, and shows the figure (Core p.154). No roll or modifier is derived from it. If the Engineer is falling behind, that is yours to rule.

Arriving changes nothing

A jump debits the fuel, and that is all it writes (see @UUID[Compendium.mgt2.guide.JournalEntry.3wd9e5Iz4A9besSS.JournalEntryPage.LcZgrmow2Emk0b44]{Voyage and jump}). Arriving at a world does not put anybody ashore or close any contract. The far end of a route is two actions you take on the ship: handing over freight and settling passengers, each with its own control and its own card. A late delivery is measured on the day you settle it.

Distance is typed

The parsecs of a voyage leg are a number you enter. Either end of a leg may be a bare name with no world behind it, so the system cannot depend on working them out. Where both ends are placed worlds, the distance between them is shown beside your figure as a readout, and your figure is the one that counts.

For the same reason there is no route planner. Jump paths across a sector are a pathfinding problem, and the system keeps no index of which world can reach which.

No backup and no JSON export

The system adds no import or export of a compendium to a file, and no backup control. Foundry's Setup screen already backs up a whole world, its packs included, and restores it. A JSON file would only add portability, and it would carry the paths of your images rather than the images.

Where the book has no rule, the card stops

Some printed numbers have no printed consequence, and those are shown and left alone.

A fleet battle's Hull critical. The critical is stored on the ship at its severity. The percentage it inflicts is neither rolled nor shown (High Guard p.120), because the chapter gives no rule for the cascade that applying it would start.

An augment's Improvement. The printed cell holds several incompatible kinds of thing (Core p.106), so it stays a line of text. What an augment actually does is declared in the fields beside it, and the system computes those.

A world's law level. The sheet stores and prints it, and it draws no list of banned items. That list is book text with no numbers under it.

The Companion's vacuum table. Its text can be read as cumulative, and that reading would make a punctured suit tend towards immunity. The system reads the flat table (Companion p.67), which reproduces every printed cell. Which book's procedure applies is the rule How vacuum exposure is worked out.

Smaller things

A stash has no create button. Things enter a stash by being dragged there, as with a container.

A space scene draws no range rings. Its two transition Regions already show every range level's boundary to every player.

Nothing here prints rules text. The system cites the book and page and applies the procedure. The prose stays in the book you own. @UUID[Compendium.mgt2.guide.JournalEntry.3wd9e5Iz4A9besSS.JournalEntryPage.XAy8tHQw02RmRtPC]{Character creation} shows what this means in practice: careers, species and tables are documents you supply.
